modules/temco-docs/extension-design.title: Extension design
modules/temco-docs/extension-design.html:
Layout superseded. The views, the Pages tree behaviour and the flow are defined in ../../ui/redesign.md. Files such as home.ts and views.ts mentioned below do not exist; the code is under extensions/temco-docs/src/.

Responsibilities, one file each#

Module Owns
src/registry.ts reading docs/help/registry.json and the generated index.json/page-meta.json, the page id → file rule, the structural checks, the counts. No VS Code UI beyond Uri, WorkspaceFolder and the filesystem
src/tree.ts the Content view: which nodes exist, what they show, what a click does
src/diagnostics.ts which issues become Problems, and on which file
src/extension.ts activation, the view and status bar, the commands, the file watcher, and the model it publishes to other modules (src/api.ts)
src/store.ts what this module reads of temco-store — the catalog, the selection, the slug rule — in one file, and the only place that crosses modules
src/ui.ts what it reads of temco-ui — where a page of ours opens, and what a command argument names
src/projects.ts what it knows of temco-projects — one signal, so the Library's rows come back when a project changes
src/repositories.ts what it reads of temco-repositories — a source's code files, the material for a draft, and the repository's own scripts
src/api.ts what this module publishes: the documentation model temco-ai reads (the sets, the pages, the selection, the editor column, one change signal)
src/aiModule.ts what this module knows of temco-ai: whether it is installed, its commands, and the two calls it makes when it is (a draft, an analysis)
src/builds.ts the product repo's own builds, invoked as VS Code tasks and judged by the artifact they leave — never by an exit code, and never the form that deploys
src/report.ts the staleness report: what needs attention, grouped by owner, as Markdown. Counts rather than lists for the pages that have merely never been reviewed
src/scaffold.ts starting a registry in an open folder that has none: the smallest valid file, on a confirmation, with the seeding left to the repository's own generator
src/home.ts the dashboard: the one page that is not about a folder — identity, how the application works, what exists now, how to start, and every feature with its state
src/views.ts the other two sidebar sections: Work (what needs doing, and what changed) and Library (what it reads and produces)
src/feedback.ts feedback rows routed to their page's owner, against a proposed file shape, with the aging called out
src/previewPanel.ts the page as a reader sees it, in its own editor tab beside the source: one panel per document, redrawn as the page is typed. Rendering is the built-in Markdown pipeline, so the preview and the editor's own idea of the page cannot disagree; the DocFX > [!NOTE] markers are dressed as the alerts the site publishes
src/diffPage.ts the page against its last commit, in vscode.diff. HEAD's text is read with git show, written under the extension's storage, and deleted when the tab closes. The right-hand side is the editor's buffer, so an unsaved change is part of the diff it shows
src/outline.ts the Page pane: the page's headings as a nested jump list, and its word count in the status bar. Fenced blocks are skipped, because a # inside a code sample is a comment
src/fluentEditor.ts Temco Markdown: the authoring surface — the page as a document on Fluent UI, with capture and annotation in the surface. The default editor for *.md; it owns the view type and the open command, and nothing of the protocol
src/markdownEdits.ts what bold, a list, a heading, a table and an image mean, as pure transforms over text and offsets — plus the writing behaviours (continueList, indentLines) and the search (findMatches, replaceAll). Both editors call it — Monaco through src/format.ts, the Fluent surface directly — so the two cannot drift into producing different files
src/attachments.ts where an image lands: the media/ folder, the NN-slug name, the size limit, the width warning, and the record beside it. One path for the Monaco command, the surface's paste, a capture and a file picked from disk
src/attachmentRecord.ts that record as data — parse, serialise, add a caption, decide what is stale — with no vscode import, which is what makes the rule testable
webview/docs/main.tsx that surface's shell, its caret rules, its paste matrix, its caption question, its outline, its find bar and its view modes; annotate.tsx is the canvas annotator beside it, highlight.ts the colour behind the text, find.tsx and outline.tsx the two panels, theme.ts the --vscode-* → Fluent token bridge, markdown.ts the page renderer
scripts/check-fluent.mts the content-library boundary: only webview/docs may import @fluentui. npm run check-fluent
scripts/check-docs.mts the Fluent surface's bundle loaded into a DOM and driven the way the host drives it — it renders, ready is posted once, the formatting actions produce the right Markdown, an identical set disturbs nothing, an outside change still arrives. npm run check-docs
scripts/check-record.mts the attachment record through a table of cases, including the one that matters: a picture with no recorded version is never called stale. npm run check-record
tsconfig.webview.json the webview sources type-checked on their own, since tsconfig.json covers the extension host only. npm run check-types
scripts/check-learn.mts the Temco Learn portal: what a manifest.json means, and what the page it writes says. The first coverage of a file written on every publish and read by nobody. npm run check-learn
src/learnPage.ts the portal page and the manifest rules, as pure functions — no vscode, so the publish path has something to test
src/webviewText.ts the bridge every webview surface shares: one WorkspaceEdit per save, line endings preserved, the echo guard, the capture handshake, and the bar actions (preview / diff / source / properties). Nothing that could corrupt a file is decided twice
src/csv.ts CSV as a grid can hold it and back again: RFC 4180 quoting, delimiter and end-of-line detected, and the quoting style preserved per cell so a one-cell edit is a one-line diff. No VS Code here at all
src/gridEditor.ts Grid mode: a CSV edited as cells (Univer). Same bridge as webviewText.ts; the file stays line-per-row because csv.ts does the writing
scripts/build-webview.mts the one bundler step: webview/grid.ts → out/webview/grid/ and webview/docs/main.tsx → out/webview/docs/. tsc cannot do this — the surfaces are browser code with npm dependencies

It no longer has a src/catalog/ or a src/selected.ts: the database, the selection and the slug rule are temco-store's, reached through src/store.ts.

registry.ts is deliberately free of presentation: it is the part that would survive replacing the view, and the part any other module reuses to know what pages exist — temco-ai reads it through the exported model rather than through this folder.

The tree#

Text
Content                        (view container: Temco Docs)
├─ Gaps (12)                   only when something is wrong, across all open repos
├─ T3000Webview-EEZ-Studio     only when more than one folder is open
│  ├─ t3000                    title · audience · noindex
│  │  ├─ api-reference         chapter, with a page count
│  │  │  ├─ Data Points API     owner · ship · reviewed, plus its issues as children
│  │  │  └─ …
│  │  └─ …
│  └─ legacy
└─ …
  • Counts live on the parents, because "which area needs attention" is the real question.
  • A page with issues is collapsible and its children are the reasons.
  • A page's tooltip carries what the generator knows and the registry does not: its last change, its headings, and — marked in the description and the icon — whether its code moved on since the last review. With index.json/page-meta.json absent, that block is simply missing and nothing else changes.
  • Clicking a page opens the file; if the file does not exist, the click offers to create it.
  • Areas and chapters are never empty: an area declared in areas{} with no pages still appears, which is itself information.

The page in the editor#

The editor of record is VS Code's own, deliberately. 15-online-editor.md rejects a rich editor for these files on a reason that survives checking: the pages are written one paragraph per source line (measured: 95 characters on average, 168 lines over 200), so an editor that re-wraps rewrites every paragraph it touches and a one-word change becomes a whole-file diff. What was missing was never the engine — it was the chrome around it.

Surface What it is Why not something new
the toolbar src/format.ts, on editor/title and in the context menu Monaco has no formatting bar; the buttons edit the buffer and undo like typing
Preview previewPanel.ts, a tab beside the source (preview: <page>.md) VS Code shows a page, the build shows an alert; the panel dresses the markers so the two agree
Diff diffPage.ts, vscode.diff against HEAD the editor's own diff, so the hunks seen are the hunks the pull request carries
the Page pane outline.ts: headings as a nested jump list, plus a word count in the status bar line, column, encoding and end-of-line are already the status bar's, so nothing repeats them
Grid gridEditor.ts + webview/grid.ts: a CSV as cells, reached by Open in the Grid the file stays CSV, one row per line, so a one-cell edit stays a one-line diff
Temco Markdown fluentEditor.ts + webview/docs/: the page as a document on Fluent UI, with capture and annotation built in — the default for *.md see The Fluent Markdown surface below
Temco Editor not this module any more: the page editor is extensions/temco-editor (temcoEditor.markdown), and Open in Temco Editor asks for it by command see temco-editor

One bridge, two surfaces#

Record. This is the period when temco-docs shipped two editing surfaces at once. It ended: Temco Markdown is gone, the page surface became its own module, and the shared bridge went with it (temco-editor). What is left here is only the grid.

Two editors over one file is a decision, not an accident: what you see while editing is a real choice, and it cannot be both. A source-visible editor (Temco Markdown) is the only way to be sure git diff will show what you did; a WYSIWYG editor (Temco Editor) is the only way to write a table without thinking about pipes. Everything else about them is shared, and it is shared in code, not by convention:

Shared, in the bridge (src/webviewText.ts, now temco-editor/src/bridge.ts) Why it cannot be per-surface
the ordered-write guard (a set of texts asked for, not just the newest) a write that lands late looks like an outside change, and answering it moves the caret to the end of the page
the file's own line endings a browser only has \n; writing that into a CRLF file is a whole-file diff for one word
one WorkspaceEdit over the whole file so Ctrl+Z undoes an edit rather than a keystroke, and the dirty dot means the same thing
the capture pipeline (image, pastedImage, capture, commitCapture, caption, linkPage) the picture lands beside the page with its words and its version; two copies of that would drift
the surface-failure reporter in the HTML an editor that cannot start must say so in its own tab — an empty one is the failure a person cannot act on

PageEditor is therefore 30 lines: it names the bundle (page) and nothing else. Two surfaces, one set of rules. The ribbon is the second half of that: .ribbon lives in temco-ui/media/page.css, so both editors wear the same strip.

A surface that asks a question draws the question itself. A webview frame is sandboxed without modals, so window.prompt returns null there — the Link button was dead for exactly that reason, and the page now asks in the vocabulary's own box (.page-surface__ask), where Enter accepts and Escape cancels.

The controls both surfaces need live in webview/shared/: find.tsx (the bar; replacement is optional, because a rich document cannot truthfully "replace text" across formatting), outline.tsx (a jump list whose target is called at — a line for a source surface, a document position for a rich one), annotate.tsx (the canvas annotator) and surface-controls.css. They were inside webview/docs/ until the page needed them; a copy in each surface is how the two would drift.

The page's chrome: a document application, not a card#

The rich page is arranged the way a document application is, because that is what it is: Home · View at the top, groups under each, a sheet on a canvas, and a status strip. Two tabs and not three: there are about twenty controls, and the insert ones (link, picture, screenshot, table) are part of writing, so they sit on Home beside the marks and the block commands. View is what reads the page or hands it to another surface. A third tab for six controls was a tab nobody visits, and it made every control a guess about which of the two tabs held it.

Element Rule Why
the ribbon flush to the tab: no border on three sides, no corners, border-bottom only a card floating in a window is a page; a document's ribbon is part of the window
the controls 30 px icon buttons, 20 px glyphs, 44 px panel, no group captions a writing bar should cost as little vertical space as possible; the captions are dropped because a caption under every group is a teaching aid a narrow editor pane cannot afford — the hairline between groups and each control's tooltip carry the same information. Only an icon-only control gets a square (btn--icon); a word button keeps its own width, which is what stops two of them drawing on top of each other
density full ≥ 940 px, compact below — measured, not guessed 905 px is what the whole Home tab needs (83 history + 215 marks + 128 style + 128 lists + 149 blocks + 182 insert + hairline and padding). A compact bar keeps nine controls and folds five into ⋯. Every group declares its controls once, with a tier, and ⋯ is the same table with the tier-2 rows taken out — an overflow menu written by hand is a second copy that drifts
the sheet .page-surface__paper: no border, no radius, on .page-surface__canvas, min-height: calc(100% - 16px) a sheet is a sheet; the canvas is a plain scroll container, not a flex row — a flex item is stretched to the container's height, which cut the sheet off at the fold and let the rest of the document spill onto the grey
one paragraph style the Text menu names the block the caret is in and sets it; there is no second row of Normal / Heading 1–3 buttons two controls for one thing made the bar teach two ways to do it, and the buttons pushed the insert group off a narrow pane
zoom − 100% + in the status strip, a view only it never reaches the file, which is why it can exist at all
Find / Outline Find is on the View tab; the outline is a rail on the right with its toggle at the far right of Home and Ctrl+Alt+O anywhere navigating a document is not editing it — but a table of contents is used while writing, so its toggle lives where the writing is. Right, not left: the rail is the TOC the published page shows, so the structure you edit is the structure you ship
the outline as a tree nesting from src/outlineModel.ts (scripts/check-outline.mts proves it): a heading hangs off the nearest one above it with a lower level, however many levels are skipped; the row the caret is in is marked current; folding is per row and remembered; the filter keeps the branch that leads to a match a list of indented headings cannot say "this belongs to that", and a ### after a # is a real document, not an error. The model is pure so the three rules that fail silently — a skipped level, a branch that springs open while typing, a caret with no current row — are checked without a browser
the outline rail 300 px by default, docked on the right, dragged by its divider (180–560 px, arrow keys too) and remembered in the webview state; never floated the width is a preference, so it is set by hand once rather than guessed at; the two limits are what stop a drag from eating the page. It is Ctrl+Alt+O away if it is in the way
a toggle that is on the glyph takes the accent, a hairline ring says pressed — never a filled block a block of the selection colour reads as a button that was just clicked, not as a mode that is on. Bold, italic, Find, Outline and the rail all use it, so an "on" looks the same wherever it is
the rail opens itself on a page with three or more headings, once, and never again for someone who closed it (outline: undefined means "never asked") a TOC of one line is furniture; a rail that reopens itself after being closed is a fight
Read mode View → Read the page: a second engine (reading.tsx) over the same seam, no caret, no editing tabs reading a page should not be one keystroke from changing it; and it is the proof that the seam is real
Link · Picture · Screenshot · Table the Home tab, beside the marks: a link and a picture are what writing a page is made of Word's Insert tab exists for the fifty things Word can insert; six do not earn a tab. The horizontal rule, which used to be in two tabs, is now in one place
Annotate Home, enabled only when a picture is selected, and it replaces that picture the page keeps one figure, not a pair

What is deliberately not in this ribbon: font, font size, text colour, alignment, spacing, margins. Markdown cannot hold them, and a control whose effect disappears on the next save is a lie — the same reason the alignment group was removed from the source surface.

The editor's three files, and the seam between them#

Text
webview/page/
  main.tsx       409  the mount: host protocol, the document, find/outline/zoom/status
  ribbon.tsx     311  the bar: tabs, groups, gallery, overflow      ← imports no Tiptap
  document.tsx   297  the engine: extensions, usePageDocument, actionsFor, stateOf
  reading.tsx     50  a second engine that cannot edit             ← proves the seam

Where this is now. The three files moved to extensions/temco-editor/webview/markdown/ when the editor became its own module, and the seam was separated from the engine: the two types below live in contract.ts (no package named in it), and document.tsx sits under engine/tiptap/ with bubble.tsx, handle.tsx and taskLists.mts. Everything this section says about the seam still holds; only the paths changed. temco-docs keeps webviewText.ts' share of the work as src/webview.ts, which is now just webviewAssets for the grid.

The seam is two types, both in document.tsx:
PageState what is true at the caret — block, marks, lists, inTable, onImage, link, canUndo, canRedo, words
PageActions named operations — setBlock, toggleMark, setLink, insertImage, replaceImage, goto, load, content, node…

grep -r "@tiptap" webview/page/ribbon.tsx webview/shared/ returns nothing, which is the property worth keeping: the bar can be re-skinned without touching the engine, and the engine replaced without touching a button. Read mode is the proof — it hands the same PageRibbon a frozen READING_ACTIONS and static markup instead of an editor, and the bar draws itself exactly as before with its editing tabs removed.

One trap the split exposed, recorded because it will catch the next person: an actions facade built on every render makes the host-message effect re-subscribe on every keystroke, and the document that arrived while the effect was detached is lost — the page then opens with stale text. The facade is one object per editor (useMemo on the editor instance).

The three optional surfaces are webviews, so they need a bundler — the only one in this extension:

Text
webview/grid.ts       ──esbuild──▶  out/webview/grid/grid.js      11.9 MB  Univer (Apache-2.0)

The page surface has its own bundler in its own module (extensions/temco-editor, out/webview/markdown/), because a module builds what it owns.

Where this belongs: the extension, and what moving it into core would take#

The surfaces are an extension today. The question "should this be product code instead" has a factual answer in this fork, so it is recorded here rather than argued:

Extension (extensions/temco-docs) Core (src/vs/workbench/contrib/…)
how a surface is registered customEditors contribution + registerCustomTextEditorProvider an EditorPane on EditorExtensions.EditorPane with its own EditorInput + IEditorSerializer; the in-tree templates are contrib/imageCarousel (pane + webview) and contrib/update/releaseNotesEditor (a webview editor)
what it can reach the public API: vscode.* every service: IEditorService, IStorageService, IFileService, IContextKeyService, INotificationService, the chat/agent services, MenuRegistry, ViewsRegistry
tab restore retainContextWhenHidden, a webview kept alive in a hidden tab the editor input serializes itself, so a tab comes back without the hack
iteration edit, npm run build-webview, reload the window edit, client compile, repo gates
price of a change local and quick valid-layers-check, layering rules, a full client compile

Two things decide it. A core surface cannot import React, Tiptap or Fluent — src/vs has no React and no JSX toolchain — so the content would still be a webview bundle whatever we do; only the host moves. And the fork already contains the pattern for that split (imageCarousel: DOM in core, a webview for what needs one).

The target, when the surfaces stop being experimental:

Text
src/vs/workbench/contrib/temcoDocs/
  browser/
    temcoDocs.contribution.ts        registers the panes, commands, menus, views

The migration is worth doing when one of these is true: a surface needs a workbench service an extension cannot see (the editor group layout, the chat context, a real IStorageService), tab restore has to be exact, or the module needs its own keybindings and menus without the when-clause traps. Until then the extension is not a limitation being tolerated — it is the cheapest place to keep a surface that is still being designed, and everything above it (the round trip, the capture pipeline, the page model) is already plain TypeScript that moves without a rewrite.

The output goes to out/webview/, beside the extension host JavaScript and inside the directory this repository already treats as build output, so it is ignored by git. It is deliberately not committed: the local/code-no-new-javascript-files rule rejects a newly added .js, and only a CODEOWNERS edit can allowlist one. vscode:prepublish runs the build for a packaged extension, so a source tree needs npm run build-webview once.

What was tried and removed: the rich editor#

The page was once offered twice: the source surface, and a Rich mode built on the official Tiptap UI Components template — 161 vendored files, 21 @tiptap/* packages and a 1.6 MB bundle. It was removed, because:

  • The file is the source of truth, and it is Markdown. The site, the offline help and the AI context all read it, and review is a git diff of one paragraph per line. A ProseMirror document has to be serialised back, and a round trip that re-wraps a paragraph turns a one-word edit into a whole-file diff — which is the failure this whole document exists to avoid.
  • It cost more than it gave. Four extensions had to be removed because they do not survive that round trip (TextAlign, Subscript/Superscript, Typography, colour highlight), each one a standing risk that the repairs in tidy() cannot keep up. Two editors was also two sets of interactions to keep right, and the one that showed the document as a document was never the one that showed the bytes.
  • It did not look like the product. It wore the template's own chrome rather than page.css, so the two editors did not resemble each other, let alone the rest of the application.

What it taught is kept, because it is the reason the shipped surface has the caret rules it has: a set that replaces the document under the caret moves the caret to the end of the page, an echo of the editor's own write must be dropped rather than applied, and applyEdit landing out of order makes a late write of ours look like an outside change. Those three lessons are enforced in webview/docs/main.tsx and asserted in check-docs and in the scenario below.

The rich page: Tiptap, and the round trip that makes it safe#

Where it lives now. This surface became its own module: extensions/temco-editor, view type temcoEditor.markdown, and it is the default for *.md today. The paths below are the ones it had while it lived here; the reasoning, the rules and the checks are unchanged and still apply — see temco-editor for the current tree. The two-surface comparison this section describes is over: the winning affordances (a selection menu, a block handle, a placeholder) are in that module, the losing prototype was deleted, and the ribbons of the two surfaces became one.

The rich editor is back, and it is the same engine — Tiptap, then 3.30.3 and now 3.32, twelve packages, its own bundle at 983 KB (1457 KB today, with Fluent, Radix and the drag handle).

Part What it was Where it is now
src/pageMarkdown.ts the whole contract: toHtml (marked), toMarkdown (turndown + GFM), roundTrip temco-editor/src/markdown.ts
webview/page/main.tsx the Tiptap editor and its ribbon; it never sees a file, only Markdown over the message port temco-editor/webview/markdown/main.tsx
webview/page/taskLists.mts Tiptap's TaskList/TaskItem, extended to accept the shape marked writes as well as their own temco-editor/webview/markdown/engine/tiptap/taskLists.mts
pageEditor.ts temcoDocs.page, a CustomTextEditorProvider on the same text document the source surface edits temco-editor/src/surfaces/markdown.ts (temcoEditor.markdown)

scripts/check-task-lists.mts the two task-list shapes, through a real editor in jsdom: open, save, and the lists that must not be claimed temco-editor/scripts/check-task-lists.mts

The rules the conversion needs, each one a case in check-page:

  • Tiptap wraps a table in <colgroup>; the GFM rule only recognises a table whose first child is a row, so a table would serialise as raw HTML and the file would lose it. The colgroup is dropped — column widths are the reader's.
  • A paragraph inside a list item or a table cell emits no blank line. With one, a tight list becomes loose and every bullet is rewritten, and a table row breaks into fragments.
  • Turndown pads a bullet marker to the width of the longest marker in the list (- one), so markers are collapsed back to one space. A task item's checkbox is followed by one space, not two.
  • *italic* is written *italic*, not _italic_; the GFM plugin's strikethrough writes a single ~, which is not strikethrough at all, so it is overridden to ~~.
  • Underline and highlight have no Markdown spelling. They are kept as the inline HTML Markdown already allows (<u>, <mark>), because a button whose effect disappears on the next save is a lie.
  • A task list is two shapes, and both are accepted. marked writes - [x] done as <ul><li><input type="checkbox" checked> done</li></ul>; Tiptap renders it as ul[data-type="taskList"] > li[data-type="taskItem"] with the checkbox inside a <label>. Without a rule for each direction the checkbox was lost twice — the page opened as a plain bullet list, and an item that did survive saved as - done. engine/tiptap/taskLists.mts adds the second shape to the parser, and the taskCheckbox rule in src/markdown.ts reads the checkbox wherever it sits. check-task-lists.mts drives a real editor over both shapes; check-page.mts keeps the serialised result byte-identical.
  • Alignment and colour are not in the toolbar. A paragraph's alignment lives in a style attribute Markdown cannot hold, which is the same reason table widths are not kept. The reader decides both.

The two surfaces are peers over one file, not two products: the tab's menu reaches the other one (temcoDocs.page.open, Open With…), and both write the same document, so save, the dirty dot, Ctrl+Z and git diff mean the same thing in either. The Markdown source surface stays the default for *.md; a workspace that wants the page instead changes one priority in package.json, or a person picks it once in Open With….

The two editors also share one ribbon: .ribbon and its groups live in temco-ui/media/page.css, so the strip a writer recognises in the source surface is the strip in the page, drawn from the same buttons and badges.

The engine and the design language: both stay#

Two questions come back often enough to answer once.

Tiptap is not the editor; it is the document model. It owns the schema, the text, the caret, the undo history and the HTML — engine/tiptap/document.tsx (the schema and the editor) and engine/tiptap/taskLists.mts (the two task-list shapes) are the only files in the product that import @tiptap/*. Everything that a person sees or presses is ours: ribbon.tsx, main.tsx, outline.tsx, find.tsx, and the round trip in src/markdown.ts, which converts HTML ⇄ Markdown with marked/turndown and has no Tiptap import at all. The contract between the two is PageState (a snapshot) and PageActions (named operations), and reading.tsx runs the same ribbon, outline and status strip behind an implementation with no editor, which is the seam being real rather than drawn. Since the move, the contract is its own file (webview/markdown/contract.ts) and names no package at all.

Swapping the engine is therefore possible and pointless: it would rewrite those 315 lines, change no button, and re-prove the behaviour check-page already proves. Tiptap earns its place at roughly a third of the bundle, because a rich-text model with tables, task lists, images, marks and undo is not a weekend's work.

Fluent is not the design language either. It supplies the icons (plain SVGs, no provider needed, five files) and one dialog — the annotator, ten Fluent components plus the FluentProvider that gives it the editor's light or dark theme. The ribbon, the menus (Radix, for positioning), the outline tree, the sheet and the status strip are the vocabulary's own HTML and CSS. scripts/check-fluent.mts fails the build if anything outside webview/markdown, webview/shared (in temco-editor) imports it, so a second design language cannot creep in unnoticed. Removing Fluent entirely would mean replacing those glyphs and one dialog — worth doing when the annotator next needs a change, not before.

What was removed: ONLYOFFICE#

src/office/ (sign, config, bridge, desktop paths, the custom editor), its four commands, its settings block and scripts/check-office.mts were deleted. ONLYOFFICE Docs does edit .md natively and the integration worked, but the licence and the deployment each decide the question on their own:

  • AGPL-3.0. The Document Server is a network service; serving it to our own users is exactly the case the licence covers, and embedding it in a desktop product does not avoid that.
  • A server nobody has. It is not a library — it is a Docker or WSL deployment with its own storage, callback URLs and JWT signing. No such server exists in this repository or on the machines this product runs on, and a document editor that needs one before it can open a file is not a desktop product.

Tiptap answers the same need — a document, in the product, offline, on the file — with a licence we can ship.

Importing Word documents#

src/docx.ts + src/docxConvert.ts: mammoth reads the .docx into semantic HTML and turndown turns that into Markdown, in a child process so the extension host never blocks. The result is a starting point — Word's fonts, colours, spacing and text boxes have no Markdown equivalent and are dropped rather than faked — which is why it writes a new page beside the document instead of replacing anything.

The converter is TypeScript, compiled to out/docxConvert.js and spawned from there. It is deliberately not a .mjs beside the sources: the repository's pre-commit hook rejects a newly added JavaScript file, and scripts/** is excluded from the packaged extension, so a script there would convert Word documents from a source tree and fail from an installed one.

Tiptap's own DOCX extensions were considered and are not used: both need a paid subscription and a private registry, and import runs on Tiptap's cloud with a JWT.

Both are iife and self-contained: a webview has no module loader and there is no CDN, so everything a surface needs travels with it. npm run build-webview writes both (esbuild + Sass) into out/webview/, which is ignored by git — so a source tree needs that one command before the editor or the Grid surface will open, and vscode:prepublish runs it for a packaged extension. No network and no npm install are needed after that build.

What neither surface owns: the document. Both send the whole file text to the extension, which applies it as a single WorkspaceEdit — so Ctrl+Z, the dirty dot, save, Diff and the git gutter keep working exactly as they do in the source editor.

Not built: a grid for .xlsx. It is a binary file that git cannot diff and that needs an .xlsx parser of its own (the maintained options are either deprecated on npm or drag in a pro tier), so a workbook keeps opening as what it is — a binary — rather than behind a grid that pretends it can be reviewed.

The Grid surface: a spreadsheet over CSV#

webview/grid.ts is Univer, bundled the same way the page is; src/gridEditor.ts is its host. The contract is deliberately narrow: the host sends { type: 'set', rows } with what parseCsv read, the surface sends back { type: 'change', rows } once an edit settles, and the host writes that through writeCsv as one WorkspaceEdit. The cells are plain strings and the quoting is the extension's, so a one-cell change stays a one-line diff.

Four things about it are worth keeping written down, because each one cost an afternoon and none of them fails loudly:

  • The event is the workbook's. In Univer 1.2.0 onCommandExecuted belongs to FWorkbook, not to the application. The first version guarded typeof api.onCommandExecuted === 'function', which is false in every build, so the surface never reported anything: the grid accepted a cell edit, displayed it, and saved nothing.
  • A sheet is 1000 × 20 unless told otherwise. getRange past the sheet's own size throws Range is out of bounds, so the read is clamped to getMaxRows()/getMaxColumns() and the workbook is created at least as large as the file it is given. Reading Math.max(200, maxRows) columns was asking for a range that did not exist.
  • Univer runs commands continuously — selection, scroll, render. A debounce that clears its own timer on every command therefore never fires; the timer is armed once and allowed to run, and flush() decides whether anything really changed by comparing against the last thing it sent.
  • A throw inside a timer is invisible. Reading the cells happened in the settle callback, so its exception became an unhandled page error and the surface simply stopped reporting. Both the read and the flush say so with console.error.

src/cells.ts holds the parts that need no browser — asRows, widthOf, trimCells — so scripts/check-grid.mts can prove the round trip without a window: a file opened and not edited reproduces itself byte for byte, and one edited cell stays one line.

The preview and the diff are tabs of the editor group, not tabs inside one pane. A custom editor that owned the document would have to bundle its own Monaco, and every copy of Monaco is worse than the one this window is already running: no git gutter, no search results landing on the right line, no other extension's decorations. The Source │ Preview │ Diff strip in the design is therefore three sibling tabs, which is also what VS Code's own Markdown preview does.

Which editor opens what:

File Opens in
.md Temco Markdown, by default — one Open With… → Text Editor away from the source, and the file never changes meaning
.csv, .tsv the text editor — or the Grid, on request
.xlsx whatever VS Code opens a binary with; there is no grid for it (see above)
everything else untouched — the ordinary VS Code editor

One editor per kind, on purpose. There is no second rich-text surface for .md: the file is the source of truth and it is already readable in the surface's Page view, so an engine between the person and the bytes buys formatting they cannot review in a diff. The Office question is settled the same way, in ../../platform-design.md: .docx/.xlsx/.pptx are not edited in the product — Word documents come in through src/docx.ts, and an OOXML editor would make the source of truth binary, un-diffable, and (ONLYOFFICE being AGPL-3.0) unshippable.

Writing, not just Markdown#

Four behaviours exist because a page of instructions is written in a list, edited in place and read back:

Behaviour Why
Enter inside a list starts the next item, numbering included, and Enter on an empty item ends the list every step is typed as an item; making each one by hand is the most repeated keystroke in the page
Tab / Shift+Tab indent and outdent the selected lines a nested step is two spaces, and nothing else should move
the colour behind the words see below — the input stays a textarea, so none of the caret rules are put at risk for colour
the caret is revealed after a jump the outline moves the caret into a line that may be off screen, and a caret you cannot see is a caret you do not trust

Colour without a second editor engine#

The source pane is a <textarea>, and it has to stay one: every caret guarantee in this surface rests on the native element's own selection behaviour. So the highlighting is a mirror <pre> behind the text, and the textarea's own text is transparent with only its caret and selection visible:

Text
┌───────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ <pre class="editor__mirror" aria-hidden>  ← colour, tokens, identical font  │
│ <textarea class="source">                 ← transparent text, real caret     │
└───────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Two things make or break it, and both are asserted: the mirror must hold exactly the same characters (one dropped space slides the colour out from under the words), and the control must not paint its own background — Fluent gives the textarea a surface, which is precisely what hides the colour, so that one declaration is !important on purpose. MD-10 in the scenario measures both, because neither is visible in a diff and both look fine in a type check.

The protocol#

Text
webview                              host (WebviewTextEditor)

   ├───────────────────────────────────▶│  answers with `set` — the document's own text
   │  {type:'change', text}             │
   ├───────────────────────────────────▶│  one WorkspaceEdit over the whole file, 350 ms after typing settles
   │  {type:'action', action:'capture'} │
   ├───────────────────────────────────▶│  takes the screenshot and holds it (nothing is written yet)
   │  ◀──────── {type:'captureReady'} ──┤
   │  {type:'action', action:'commitCapture', caption}

   │  ◀── {type:'image', src, alt} ─────┤  answers with a page-relative address and the words

   ├───────────────────────────────────▶│  records the words; nothing moves

   ├───────────────────────────────────▶│  runs the command **with this document's URI**

The capture is taken before the caption is asked for, and that order is deliberate: the screen a person wants is the one behind this window, and a dialog raised first would photograph the question. The bytes stay on the host while the surface asks, because a full screen is megabytes of base64 and it would cross the boundary twice for nothing.

action carries the document, because inside a custom editor there is no activeTextEditor: a command that fell back to "whatever editor is in front" would find nothing and quietly do nothing.

The caret, in the surface that ships#

The three rules learned from the rich editor's round trip hold here too, and they are enforced in the webview rather than hoped for:

Rule Why
a set exactly equal to what is on screen is dropped the common case is an echo of our own write; redrawing identical text only moves the caret
a set that is an outside change while the surface has focus is queued, applied on blur a replacement under the caret collapses the selection being dragged
an inserted image goes in at the caret, never appended "quick" means where you are, not the end of the page
ready is posted exactly once, ever the host answers ready with its own copy of the document; posting it again mid-write is what puts older text back under the caret

Validating this in real VS Code found a fourth defect that the prototype could not show, and it was the worst of the set: the message listener was re-subscribed whenever the status state changed, and each subscription posted ready again. ready makes the host answer with its own copy of the document — an answer that can arrive while a write of ours is still in flight, which puts the older text back under the caret. That is exactly the "the cursor comes to another place" report, arriving through a channel that only exists in the real host. The listener is now installed once, and the current closure is carried by a ref.

npm run check-docs now guards it headlessly: the bundle is loaded into a DOM, a set is delivered, the surface is typed into, and the run fails if ready was posted more than once. Removing the fix makes it fail (the surface reported ready, typing did not post a second ready), which is the check earning its place — no screenshot and no type check can see this.

The status badge is part of the same fix. The host never echoes a change it applied itself, so a badge that compared the page against "the text the document opened with" stayed on unsaved forever. It now means what it says — writing… while the bridge is behind, in document once the edit is in the document — and it deliberately does not duplicate "is the file saved", which is the tab's dirty dot.

Screenshots, and why the capture is host-side#

getDisplayMedia is not dependable inside a webview — the frame is not granted display capture in every build — so the capture happens where the OS window is. captureScreen() runs a small platform command (System.Windows.Forms.Screen

  • System.Drawing on Windows, screencapture -x on macOS), writes a PNG to the temp folder, and holds the bytes. Linux reports that capture is unsupported and points at the paste.

Nothing else about the pipeline is different from a paste: the bytes are written beside the page and the surface gets a relative address back.

Concern Decision
where an image lives media/ beside the page — one folder per page folder, so a page moved with its folder keeps its images
what the Markdown holds media/NN-slug.png, relative — what the build resolves, so a published page needs no rewriting
the file name NN-slug, the number continuing the folder's own sequence and the slug from the page — never image.png, and never a name that collides
two screenshots with the same name impossible: the sequence number is read from the folder
what the file receives nothing at capture time; the surface inserts the reference and the normal save path carries it in
the words one string, used as the alt text and as the visible caption. A screen reader and a reader see the same sentence, and there is no second field to fall out of step
what a picture depicts appliesTo, recorded at insert time (design §22.4, S1)

| Page | Image | Shows | Documentation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| t3000/commissioning | 01-commissioning.png | 13.0 | 13.1 |
| t3000/data-points | 02-scaled.png | 13.0 | 13.1 |

Stale is a warning, not a block. Publishing one of these is allowed, and this report is what records it.

Two silences are deliberate. An image with no appliesTo is never called stale — "we do not know" is a different claim from "this is old", and a false accusation on every page written before the record existed would make the report worthless. And no version report means no report at all, because there is nothing to compare against.

What was proven in a real window#

.build/vscode-playwright-mcp/temco-markdown-editor.cjs drives a dev build and passes sixteen steps: the surface opens, the source pane holds the file from disk, typing reaches the file after Ctrl+S, the caret is still where typing left it, re-opening the page costs zero bytes, the surface fills the editor area, a screenshot is taken and then asks what it shows, the caption becomes both the reference and the record, the preview renders it as a figure whose alt text is the same words, the colour behind the text lines up with the words, the outline lists the headings and jumps to one, find counts its matches, the view modes show one pane or both, and the tab menu's Temco Docs submenu offers the three views for this surface. The last one chooses each ribbon tab and proves the document is untouched by the choosing, because a tab is a place commands live, not a place text does. The sixteenth zooms in and measures the source against its colour mirror, then resets, because a zoom that moves one layer and not the other is invisible in every other check.

A second scenario, .build/vscode-playwright-mcp/temco-page-editor.cjs, drives the rich page and passes three steps: the page opens on the file that was in front and holds its text, typing marks the tab dirty and only Ctrl+S writes the new line to the file as Markdown, and Bold from the ribbon produces ** in the file while the heading it did not touch stays byte-identical. A fourth thing is proved outside the window: npm run check-page renders a whole page to HTML and back and requires it to come back unchanged, and the built bundle is loaded in a plain browser with a stubbed host to prove that the first answer to ready is not lost.

Three defects were found by running that scenario, and all three are fixed in the product:

Symptom Cause Fix
the editor tab was there and the area inside it was empty, with no webview at all the bundle threw at load: ColorBackground24Regular was used but never imported, and webview/page was not in tsconfig.webview.json, so nothing type-checked it the import is restored and the surface is type-checked like the other one
the page opened blank although the host had sent the text the host answers ready at once, and the answer arrived while Tiptap was still creating its editor, where the handler dropped it the answer is held in a module-level inbox and handed over when there is an editor to accept it
the scenario clicked an editor that was not on screen two tabs carried the same file name — the source surface and the page — and a hidden webview still answers a selector the page is left as the only tab, and "in front" is checked by the editor's own header naming Temco Editor

The first one is the lesson worth keeping: a webview that fails to start looks exactly like a webview that has not been caught up yet, and neither looks like an error. The try/catch in resolveCustomTextEditor exists because of it — a surface that cannot start now says so in its own tab.

A third scenario, .build/vscode-playwright-mcp/temco-docs-page-link.cjs, opens a page nested inside a documentation set. Its second step — link to a page and page properties — is reported as blocked, not passed: both read the project catalog, and the harness cannot register a project, so a folder holding docs/help/registry.json is still "Repositories with a registry: 0". Both menu items are reachable in the surface; the picker and the panel behind them are the unverified part, and registering a project in the harness is the missing capability.

Three defects were found by looking at that run's screenshots and logs rather than by its assertions, and all are fixed:

Symptom Cause Fix
the whole surface sat in a band at the top of the editor FluentProvider renders its own div inside #root; with no height every height: 100% below it collapses to nothing #root > div { height: 100% }
the source pane was 260 px tall in an 828 px pane Fluent's Textarea is a wrapper around the real <textarea>, and the control it draws is capped by its own max-height both levels fill: the wrapper is a flex box, the control takes height: 100% with max-height: none
a run failed with an empty source pane the bar paints before the document arrives, so "the editor is open" was being decided by the first paint rather than by the text the scenario waits for the file's text, which is what a person sees

The layout one is now an assertion (MD-06), because a screenshot alone does not keep it fixed.

Three harness facts are worth writing down, since they cost the most time: a webview is two frames deep (iframe.webview serves the platform's index.html, and the extension's document is the nested #active-frame); retainContextWhenHidden keeps a webview alive in a background tab, so finding its frame proves nothing about what a person can click; and on a loaded machine a cold dev build can take two minutes to activate, which is a timeout to raise rather than a bug to chase.

When a menu entry is gated on the editor, key it on the editor. Retiring the rich editor left three commands — Open in Source Mode, Preview the Page, Diff the Page with HEAD — gated on activeCustomEditorId == 'temcoDocs.richTiptap', an id that no longer existed, so they were hidden and nothing failed. Two rules came out of it, and MD-14 now enforces both:

Rule Why
activeCustomEditorId names this surface; editorLangId does not activeCustomEditorId is empty unless the active input is a custom editor, while editorLangId follows the active text editor — and a webview is not one. The built-in markdown preview keys its editor/title/context entry on resourceLangId for exactly this reason, and that difference is why the tab menu's Temco Docs submenu was invisible until it was corrected.
a when that can never be true looks exactly like a working feature Nothing errors and nothing logs. Only an assertion that the command is present tells the two apart, which is why the step opens the menu instead of trusting the manifest.

The three now live in that submenu rather than in editor/title, because the surface already draws them in its own head — as icons, next to the view modes — and a title-bar twin both repeated them and squeezed the breadcrumb. editor/title keeps only the source-mode twins keyed on editorLangId, so each action appears once in each mode.

Two deliberate deviations#

Deviation Why
Fluent lives in extensions/temco-docs/webview/docs/, not in temco-ui temco-ui has no React runtime and no JSX toolchain; extracting means giving it both. It is confined rather than unowned: scripts/check-fluent.mts fails the build if any other file imports @fluentui. The trigger to extract is a second Fluent surface.
.md opens in this editor by default it is the authoring surface. The risk of a custom editor is that it changes what the file means; this one writes Markdown through the document, so it cannot. Every other surface here stays option.

The reader: what a published version looks like#

Authoring is one half of documentation; this is the other half. A published version gets a page beside the files the generator produced, and the reader is not a second renderer: the article is the generated page in a frame, so DocFX (or MkDocs, or Docusaurus) keeps rendering its own Markdown, and the reader supplies the shape a documentation site has.

Text
┌ Temco Learn ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Temco Learn   T3000                        [13.0 ▾]        [ Search this version… ]       │
├──────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────────────────┬────────────────────┤
│ T3000 · 13.0     │ T3000 › Commissioning the T3000                   │ IN THIS ARTICLE     │
│  T3000 docs      │                                                   │  Before you start   │
│ ▸Commissioning   │ Commissioning the T3000        ← the generated    │  Terminate the pair │
│  Verify reset    │                                   page, framed    │    With one segment │
│                  │                                                   │  Verify the reset   │
│                  │ ◀ T3000 documentation        Verify the reset ▶   │                     │
├──────────────────┴───────────────────────────────────────────────────┴────────────────────┤
│ T3000 13.0                                                              3 pages           │
└───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Decision Why
one self-contained file, model embedded as JSON it works from a folder, from the loopback server, and inside a CHM alike — no fetch, no build step, no second file to keep in step
the article is a frame a Markdown renderer here would be a second implementation of the generator's job, and it would drift
the sidebar is built from the pages in the folder a doc set never has to be told about the reader, and the sidebar cannot disagree with what was published
"In this article" is read from the frame it needs same-origin, which siteServer gives; from file:// a browser refuses and the panel says nothing rather than guessing
written as temco-reader.html, never index.html the generator's own home page is not ours to overwrite
the deep link is #<href> a page can be sent to a colleague, and a reload lands on it

src/learnReader.ts is pure and scripts/check-learn.mts renders it: three columns, every page in the sidebar in order, the first page framed and marked, the version picker, no markup from a title, an empty set that still renders, and the hash deep link. Twenty checks, no browser.

The same shape inside VS Code. Page mode puts the article's own headings beside it — the rail a documentation site has, because a long page is crossed by its headings and not by scrolling. Headings are addressable: renderMarkdown writes id from slugOf, so a rail link lands on the section, levels indent, and the rail is hidden in Split, where the pane is already half a tab. check-docs asserts the links and their anchors, not the pixels.

The AI panel#

Text
Temco Docs                                     (panel: the AI, docked on the right)
├─ header        the page's title (· stale) and the model in use · offline
├─ transcript    your question, the answer as it streams, notes, errors
├─ Draft update  → opens a diff: the page on the left, the draft on the right
│                  Apply replaces the whole page — one Ctrl+Z takes it back
├─ Ask the area  → the question, with the id, title and headings of the pages around it
└─ Ask           → a question about the page on screen
  • It writes nothing by itself. A draft lands in a diff and in the panel; putting it into the page is a button, and the change is an ordinary undoable edit.
  • What reaches the model is fixed. The page's text and metadata, and for an area question the ids, titles and headings of its neighbours. No other file, no repository sweep, no credential.
  • Every draft names its prompt version, so a draft can be traced to the instructions that produced it.
  • An answer's citations are checked. A page it names becomes a chip that opens it and is dashed when the page is stale; a name that is not a page is reported rather than believed; and an area answer that named nothing is replaced by search results instead of a synthesis.
  • With nothing installed the panel still opens and says what to download, so the extension never looks broken — the AI is optional the whole way down.

The dashboard, and why this repository does not have one#

00-architecture.md puts the dashboard on the site, not in the editor: a generated static page at /_admin/ — coverage · stale by owner · docs-owed · unowned · unreviewed · broken links · feedback · health score — noindex, out of the PDF, the CHM and the offline zip, built by the product repository's own pipeline (13-implementation-plan.md step 1.19). Its rows deep-link into the editor, and that hand-off is this extension's half of it.

An earlier phase built an organisation read here instead — a repository list over the GitHub API and a sidebar view — which answered the dashboard's own question more weakly (repository-level facts, none of the page-level health) and in a second place. Both are deleted, along with the token setting they needed. The rule is the same one this document already carries for checks: the extension never computes an answer the product repository already owns.

Commands#

Command Does
temcoDocs.showStatus refreshes, writes the full report to the Temco Docs output channel, offers Show Problems
temcoDocs.validate same, and is what the status-bar item and the view title button call
temcoDocs.refresh re-reads the registries
temcoDocs.openRegistry opens registry.json for the folder the node belongs to
temcoDocs.openPage opens the page, or offers to create the missing file
temcoDocs.markdown opens the page in Temco Markdown, the Fluent authoring surface — the way back in from the source editor
temcoDocs.staleScreenshots the report of pictures a newer version has left behind, from the record beside each page's images. Nothing is written and nothing is refused (design §22.4, S3)
temcoDocs.reveal shows the page's file — or a chapter's, an area's or a source's folder — in the operating system's file manager (revealFileInOS, not the VS Code view of a similar name)
temcoDocs.openTerminal opens an integrated terminal at the folder that row stands for
temcoDocs.copyPath · copyRelativePath the row's path on the clipboard, absolute or relative to the open folder
temcoDocs.newPage · newChapter a page (kind, title, file name) or a chapter — a folder with its first page, since an empty chapter does not exist
temcoDocs.newPage.article · .task · .reference · .troubleshooting · .releaseNote the same as newPage with the kind already named, so the New Page of a Kind submenu is one click per kind
temcoDocs.renamePage the title as a registry value, and the page's first # with it — never the file name
temcoDocs.movePageUp · movePageDown a two-number swap of order in registry.json
temcoDocs.retirePage deprecated and superseded_by; the file stays, so old links keep redirecting
temcoDocs.buildSite invokes the repository's own docs:site as a task and reports the files it produced
temcoDocs.buildHelp invokes the non-deploying help build (build:help:dry) and reports the CHM it produced
temcoDocs.stalenessReport opens the report of what is owed as an untitled Markdown document — nothing is written
temcoDocs.newPage · newChapter · the five kind commands open the New page page (src/newPagePage.ts) with the row's place and, for a kind, its kind already chosen. The page writes through writePage() — one write, one confirmation that names the file
temcoDocs.feedback reads each repository's docs/help/feedback.json, routes the rows to their owners, and calls out the aging

Where they surface: the Workspace view's title bar carries New page, New chapter and Refresh inline, and its … holds the page acts (open · reveal · terminal · copy a path · rename the title · move up · move down · retire · the New Page of a Kind submenu · the registry) plus Home and Validate — the same list the row's own right-click menu shows, which is the Library's shape and the Explorer's. A row's left click opens a page or expands a folder; a right click (or the keyboard's menu key) opens the menu; the hover carries nothing. Everything else is in the palette, where it costs no room — and startRegistry is a row in the view's empty state, so the view and the button that fixes it are never apart. There is no organisation-wide surface here by design: that question belongs to the site's generated dashboard, which this extension hands off to rather than re-implements.

What refreshes the view#

  • activation, and any workspace-folder change;
  • a change to **/docs/help/registry.json (created, changed, deleted) — it changes the shape of the tree;
  • a change to **/docs/help/index.json or **/docs/help/page-meta.json — they change the provenance the items display;
  • an explicit refresh.

Everything else, including saving a page, does not refresh: the tree describes structure, not prose.

Rules the code follows#

  • Two writes, each asked for. Reading is what the extension does; it writes in exactly two places, and only on a command that names what it will create: the empty file for a page the registry already declares, and an empty registry where a folder you have open has none. Both are files the registry's own generator already expects, and neither is ever an existing file. Nothing under _admin/ or _edit/ is written at all — the design's rule is that those are generated pages, not documentation. What it downloads — the runtime, a model, the manifest that records them — goes to its own storage folder, or to the folder a setting names, and never into a repository.
  • A diagnostic lands where the fix is — the page for a page problem, registry.json for a missing file or an unreadable registry.
  • Counts are not problems. reviewed: null and empty tag lists are normal in a 335-page registry; as warnings they would bury the faults that matter.
  • No module knows about the shell. Nothing reaches into the application's own code, by design.
  • Nothing is fetched unasked. The only network calls are the runtime and model downloads the user starts from Models and Runtime: no telemetry, no update check, no background refresh, no organisation scan. No credential is stored at all.
  • Nothing native ships. A compiled engine is per-OS; a downloaded one is not, which is what keeps one .vsix valid on every platform — the application, plain VS Code, Windows or macOS.
  • Building is not shipping. The build commands invoke the repository's own scripts and report what those scripts produced. The form that deploys into a T3000 installation is never run, and nothing is uploaded or committed.
  • A generated page is never overwritten. Which now means: nothing under _admin/ or _edit/ is written at all. The dashboard is the product repository's generated page; this extension is the deep-link target it hands off to.
  • An empty state is actionable. A view that only explains itself is a dead end, and the folder with no registry is exactly where a new product repository starts. The Content view's empty state is a row that runs Start a Registry rather than a sentence telling the reader to go and find one.
  • A process, only while it is wanted. The local server starts when something asks the AI for an answer, never at activation; it listens on loopback only; and it is stopped when idle, when its model is removed, and when the window closes. The extension holds no model in its own process, so nothing to load or unload blockingly.

Guardrails, in code#

12-ai-features.md, Guardrails, lists them; this is where each one actually lives, so it can be checked rather than trusted.

Guardrail Where it is enforced
No shipped page is edited by a model A draft opens in a diff; the page changes only when Apply draft is pressed, and then as one undoable WorkspaceEdit
No secrets, no customer data The only thing a prompt can take is a PageContext — page text, path, registry metadata — plus ids, titles and headings for an area question. No parameter exists that could carry another file, a token or a sweep of the repository
Traceable PROMPT_VERSION is printed on every draft and in the panel's model line, and a draft also names its commit range (temco-ai/src/ai/history.ts)
Degradable The panel opens with nothing installed and says what to download; the server never starts without a runtime and a model; a missing prompt file is a named error, not a stack trace; a page too large for one draft is refused rather than half-drafted
Deterministic first Staleness is read from index.json, never recomputed; the low-confidence fallback is plain term overlap; citations are resolved against the registry
Cost bounded 6 turns of history, 40 area candidates, 40 commits, 100k characters of page text, 1024 tokens per answer and 2048 per draft, --ctx-size 8192
Offline The runtime is a local process on 127.0.0.1; the only other network calls are the downloads the user starts
One content library scripts/check-fluent.mts fails if anything outside webview/docs imports @fluentui — a second Fluent surface is the trigger to extract it, not a stray import
A surface cannot corrupt a file every webview editor shares WebviewTextEditor, which owns the echo guard, the line endings and the single-WorkspaceEdit write; a surface only names its bundle, and scripts/check-grid.mts proves the CSV round trip keeps the file byte-for-byte when nothing is edited
One meaning per action every formatting action is a pure transform in src/markdownEdits.ts, called by both editors — there is no second copy to drift
The bar cannot teach a key that does nothing scripts/check-shortcuts.mts reads every shortcut: the ribbon advertises and traces it to an engine keymap, a package.json keybinding or a named shell listener; Ctrl+F and Ctrl+Shift+X were both taught and unbound when it was written
The page in front is a page, not a text editor frontUri() reads the active tab as well as activeTextEditor, because a custom editor has none; without it Properties, the capture target and every row command silently saw nothing
Every image has words, and a version landImage() is the only writer into media/; it records the caption and the version the picture depicts, and check-record proves a picture with no recorded version is never called stale

Roadmap#

Phase Adds
1 the Content view — registry, checks, gaps, status bar
2 the AI — model download, runtime, draft page updates from a commit range, ask-the-area; a local model, offline, drafts only, a human accepts
3 publishing — invokes the product repo's site build and offline help build and hands over the artifacts; it orchestrates, it does not reimplement the pipeline
4 (not a module of its own) — the documentation health report is the platform's generated page at /_admin/
5 feedback and health — intake, and the report of what is owed; the report's cadence stays in the product repo's CI

The module's design is what this document and registry-schema.md hold; the platform-wide design is design/temco-learn/.

The AI is the reason the module exists. Everything before it is what the AI needs in order to know what it is talking about.

modules/temco-docs/registry-schema.title: The registry the module reads
modules/temco-docs/registry-schema.html:
docs/help/registry.json in each product repository is the single description of that product's documentation set. This extension is a reader of it. The schema is owned by the generator in the product repo (scripts/docs-registry.mjs) — if a field ever needs to change, it changes there first and this reader follows.

Shape#

JSON
{
  "version": 1,
  "areas": {
    "t3000": { "title": "t3000", "audience": "user", "noindex": false }
  },
  "pages": {
    "t3000/api-reference/data-points": {
      "title": "Data Points API",
      "area": "t3000",
      "chapter": "api-reference",
      "order": 20,
      "audience": "user",
      "ship": true,
      "owner": "docs",
      "tags": [],
      "keywords": [],
      "help_ids": [],
      "code": [],
      "reviewed": null
    }
  }
}

Fields, and what they decide#

Field Where Meaning
areas registry the top level of the site: one entry per product area, with its default audience and whether it is excluded from the published site
pages registry every page, keyed by page id
title page the page's name, used for search, navigation and the tree
area, chapter page where the page sits; both must agree with the page id
order page position inside its chapter. Pages are ordered by it, then by title
audience page user, developer or contributing; falls back to the area's audience
ship page false keeps the page out of the shipped help build
owner page who is answerable for the page's accuracy
tags, keywords, help_ids, code page search facets, context-help ids, and the code globs a change should make the page stale. Empty is normal
reviewed page ISO date of the last human review, or null. null is a count, not a warning

Page id → file#

The page id is the path under docs/, without the extension:

Page id File that must exist
t3000/api-reference/data-points docs/t3000/api-reference/data-points.md

That single rule is what makes a page "missing" checkable, and it is why this extension never guesses at paths: the id is the path.

Generated neighbours#

The product repo also emits, and this extension may read:

  • docs/help/index.json — per page: its headings, the last commit that touched it (author, sha, date), and the generator's stale verdict.
  • docs/help/page-meta.json — the same provenance in the smaller shape the published page reads.

Neither is required. Absent, the extension works exactly as before; only provenance goes missing. A malformed one is a warning on that file — the fix is to regenerate it in the product repo — never an error, because it hides nothing else.

What the extension shows from them: a page's last change and headings in its tooltip, a stale marker on the page (description and icon), and a stale count in the repository and area tooltips plus the status report. The page's code globs are read from the same place, because that is what a Draft update's commit range is read against.

stale is read, never computed here. The verdict — a commit touched a path the page claims in code, after its last review — belongs to the product repo's generator (05-content-and-registry.md, Staleness). Two answers to that question would be worse than none, so the extension only repeats the generator's answer.

Structural checks#

Run on every refresh, cheap enough to run on 335 pages without thinking about it:

Check Severity Reported on
the page has no title error the page
area is not declared in areas{} error the page
the id disagrees with area/chapter error the page
registered, but the file does not exist error registry.json
no order warning the page
two pages share one title warning both pages
two pages share one order inside a chapter warning both pages
the registry declares no pages warning registry.json
the registry is not valid JSON error registry.json

Deliberately not checked here: prose quality, links, images and staleness. Those belong to the product repo's own gates (npm run docs:verify, the media audit, docs-owed) and to the AI phase, where a commit range can be read. Duplicating them in the extension would create two answers to one question.

The feedback file — a proposal, not a contract#

Where a feedback row comes from is not settled: the feedback design (09-feedback-subscriptions-notifications.md) assumes an endpoint on the T3000 server, while the management overview (16-overview.md) describes a different hosting model. This module reads the smallest shape that carries what routing needs, per repository:

JSON
{
  "version": 1,
  "rows": [
    { "page": "t3000/api-reference/data-points", "kind": "wrong", "note": "…", "at": "2026-09-01", "state": "open", "by": "…" }
  ]
}

page is a page id, at is an ISO date, and state is open or anything else for handled. A row whose page is not in the registry is still reported — with its id, as plain text rather than a link — because that is a finding about the row, not a reason to drop it. With no such file, Feedback by Owner says the source is not agreed rather than reporting no feedback.

This shape is the extension's proposal, and the docs owner accepts or replaces it. It is the only part of the feedback design that is not settled.

modules/temco-editor/readme.title: temco-editor
modules/temco-editor/readme.html:
The editor for a Markdown page: one module, one editor, three layers. It owns the surface and nothing about what a page is — that stays in temco-docs.

Identifiers#
Extension id temcocontrols.temco-editor
View type temcoEditor.markdown — Temco Editor, priority: "default" for *.md
Commands temcoEditor.open · temcoEditor.openSource · temcoEditor.preview · temcoEditor.diff · temcoEditor.pageProperties
Namespace temcoEditor
Storage none
Depends on temcocontrols.temco-docs (its model, through src/docs.ts)

Why it exists#

Writing a page in a text editor means thinking about pipes and asterisks; a WYSIWYG surface means writing the page. The editor used to live inside temco-docs as temcoDocs.page, next to the registry, the tree, the builds and the release report — 494 KB of documentation domain beside ~250 KB of editor. This module is that 250 KB, given its own front door.

It also replaced its own prototype: for a while there were two editors to compare. The comparison is over, the winning affordances are here — a selection menu for the marks, a drag handle beside a block, a placeholder on an empty page — and the prototype is deleted.

The three layers#

Text
the surface      main.tsx · ribbon.tsx · reading.tsx      asks for named operations, reads a snapshot of the caret
   ↕ contract    webview/markdown/contract.ts             PageState · PageActions · Mark · ListKind — types only
the engine       webview/markdown/engine/tiptap/          the only place a Tiptap package is named

The rule is enforced by reading, not by trust: grep -r "@tiptap" webview/markdown/*.tsx webview/shared/ returns nothing, scripts/check-shortcuts.mts reads the shortcuts out of engine/tiptap/document.tsx rather than assuming them, and replacing Tiptap means deleting one folder.

The host is the same shape from the other side: src/ knows a document, a panel, an edit and a line ending, and no Editor, Node, Mark, PluginKey or Transaction. What a page is — its media folder, the version it describes, the pages a link may reach — it asks temco-docs for, through src/docs.ts.

What it owns#

  • the view type, the provider, and the commands that reach it;
  • the bridge to the file: one WorkspaceEdit per save, the file's own line endings, and the ordered-write guard that keeps a caret still while two writes land out of order;
  • the Markdown contract (src/markdown.ts) — the rules that make an unedited page open and save to the same bytes;
  • the surface: the ribbon, the selection menu, the block handle, find, the outline rail, read mode, zoom, capture;
  • its bundle and the one bundler step that produces it.

What it must not own#

  • the registry, the pages model, the builds, the release report — temco-docs;
  • where an image lands. media/, the file name and the attachment record are the model's; this module supplies the bytes and the words and asks (landImage);
  • a second Markdown dialect. The round trip is one implementation. If Tiptap's own serialiser would be better, that is a change to the contract, proved by check-page first.

What was learned the hard way#

  • A task list was destroyed twice — on open, because marked writes <ul><li><input type="checkbox"> and Tiptap wants ul[data-type="taskList"]; on save, because turndown-plugin-gfm wants the <input> as the item's first child and Tiptap renders it inside a <label>. Both shapes are now accepted on the way in (engine/tiptap/taskLists.mts) and the checkbox is read wherever it sits on the way out (src/markdown.ts).
  • Tiptap merges attribute parsers over a rule's getAttrs, so checked had to be parsed in addAttributes, not in the parse rule.
  • A missing bundle is a blank tab, not an error: bridge.ts asks for markdown.js and markdown.css by name, a 404 on a script fires no onerror, and compile-extension:<name> cleans out/ before tsc — which deletes the bundle. check-surface.mts loads the built file, so a stale or missing bundle fails the gate instead of the tab.

Gates#

npm run vscode:prepublish, in order: check-commands · check-fluent · check-types (host and webview, separately) · compile · check-page (13 round-trip cases) · check-task-lists (a real editor, both shapes) · check-outline (29 cases, no browser) · check-shortcuts (every key the bar teaches is bound) · build-webview · check-surface (the built bundle in jsdom: it starts, draws the page, writes one edit back, keeps its checkboxes, and survives a round trip through Read mode).

From the repository root, npm run compile-temco builds the extensions and both webview bundles — the only correct way to rebuild after a tsc run, which cleans out/ first.
