18. Definition of done, and open decisions#

18.1 Done means#

  • [ ] Every §10 screen has its acceptance criteria met, checked in a real VS Code window.
  • [ ] Every §14.2 regression test exists and fails when its fix is removed.
  • [ ] No Fluent import outside temco-ui; the lint rule is enabled and green.
  • [ ] No --vscode-* variable is used to colour a Fluent surface directly (the bridge does it).
  • [ ] Document server down produces §4.10 states, verified by hand.
  • [ ] The extension packs and installs as a VSIX; the document server address is configured, never bundled.
  • [ ] docs/temco-platform/modules/temco-docs/extension-design.md updated with what was actually built.

18.2 Decisions still open (recommendation in brackets)#

  1. Transport — decided: support both, embedded by default, http opt-in (§4.1.4). Co-editing is therefore not in the default build, and the UI must say so (TR-4).
  2. Distribution scope — decided: internal now, may be sold later. This is exactly the case that needs the build gate in §4.1.5, because the AGPLv3 question only becomes urgent at the moment of conveyance. Next action: legal confirm of LG-1's wording before P1 ships, not before it starts.
  3. Document server edition — Community (free, concurrency limits, no white-label) or commercial. This decides whether the ONLYOFFICE logo appears in our editor. [Start Community; budget for commercial when branding matters.]
  4. Where the document server runs — one shared intranet host, or localhost Docker on every machine (§4.9). Shared is recommended: co-editing and shared review only exist with a shared server, and per-machine Docker is more setup per person, not less. [Shared intranet host; localhost for development only.]
  5. Where the asset store lives — local SQLite for a single workstation, or a shared Postgres for a team. The content and callback endpoints imply a reachable host, which argues for shared. [Shared Postgres + a small HTTP service; SQLite only for a personal profile.]
  6. Markdown host — decided: support both, remembered per asset (§4.8.1), Fluent by default. Remaining sub-question: whether temco.docs.markdown.engine should exist at all now that preferredHost covers it. [Keep it; it is the default for assets that have no explicit choice.]
  7. Whether .md and .docx may hold the same page — i.e. one asset, two formats. [No. One asset, one format. A conversion creates a new asset with a derived-from edge.]
  8. Engine fallback if AGPL blocks distribution — four routes in §4.1.7: R1 separate service, R2 commercial licence, R3 MPL engine (ZetaOffice), R4 no engine at all. [Start on A + B + R4 (author in Fluent, view via docx-preview, convert-on-import with a warning) because that ships with zero AGPL exposure; add R1 the day a host exists. Re-evaluate at the point the product is sold.]
  9. How much existing .docx must be edited in place — this, not preference, decides between R4 and R1/R2/R3 (§4.1.7.1). [Answer it with a corpus count: how many documents, and how many of them are round-tripped weekly.]

18.3 One-paragraph brief for the generator#

The brief is §23, at the end of this document, so it can name the feature under construction.

Build TEMCO Platform inside the existing VS Code fork. The shell is VS Code and must not be touched; every screen we own is a webview built with React 19 and Fluent UI v9 from extensions/temco-ui, themed by bridging --vscode-* variables into a Fluent theme. Office documents are edited by ONLYOFFICE, behind a pluggable OfficeTransport: either a Document Server embedded as a single cross-origin iframe (JWT-signed config, key derived from (assetId, revision, options), short-lived signed content URL, save callback that writes an immutable revision), or a fully embedded build with static web-apps plus x2t.wasm where conversion happens in-process and no server exists at all. Markdown has two hosts — a Fluent editor by default, the same Office host when the asset remembers that choice in preferredHost — resolved by explicit override → preferredHost → setting → format priority. The domain is five concepts — Product, Asset, Editor Host, Publication, Knowledge — and no sixth noun may appear. Every save is a revision; nothing edits in place; nothing ever shows a blank iframe.

22. The document feature — the whole flow#

Scope decision: this is the only feature we build now. Products, hardware, firmware and releases stay as data the document feature can reference; their screens come later. Everything below is needed for an author to sit down and write a page with screenshots in it, and for the page to stay correct across versions.

22.1 One pipeline for every image#

Three entrances, one path. The author never picks a format, a folder, or a filename.

Text
  ┌── clipboard ──────┐
  │ Ctrl+V (image)    │
  ├── capture ────────┤        ┌──────────────┐   ┌───────────────┐   ┌──────────────┐
  │ ⌘⇧5 / Screenshot  │───────►│  normalise   │──►│   annotate    │──►│  attachment  │
  ├── file picker ────┤        │  png, ≤1600w │   │  arrows, box, │   │  IMG-xxxx    │
  │ Attach image…     │        │  strip EXIF  │   │  redact, step │   │  sha256 id   │
  └── drag & drop ────┘        └──────────────┘   └───────────────┘   └──────┬───────┘
                                                                             │
                                                        insert at the caret  │
                                          ![Terminal after reset](att:IMG-7) ▼

Rules that make this worth building:

  • P1 An image is never a data URL in the document. It becomes an attachment with an id, and the document holds att:IMG-7. A 400 KB base64 blob inside a markdown file is how a docs repo becomes uncloneable.
  • P2 Capture, paste and file all end in the same annotation surface — the author does not get a worse experience because of where the bitmap came from.
  • P3 The attachment id is the content hash, so pasting the same screenshot twice reuses one attachment and one file on disk.
  • P4 Insertion is at the caret, never appended. The editor's selection survives, which is the whole point of "quick".
  • P5 Failure is visible: no clipboard permission, no capture permission, unsupported type — each gets a sentence naming the cause and the fallback.

│ caption [ Device list after reset                                    ]      │
│                                            [ Insert into document ]         │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  • A1 Every tool works with one drag. No property panels, no selection handles.
  • A2 Redact is not blur. Blur is shown as a convenience, but the redact tool replaces pixels with a solid block and the UI says so, because a blurred licence key is a published licence key.
  • A3 Undo undoes one operation, not the session. The author keeps working after a mistake.
  • A4 Annotations are baked into the PNG on insert. Nothing downstream has to understand them, and a reader cannot remove them.
  • A5 The caption becomes the alt text — accessibility and search for free, and it stops "image1.png" reaching a customer.
  • A6 Callout magnifies the dragged region (≈2.2×) into an inset connected by leader lines, so a small terminal value can be read on a 900 px screenshot. It samples the pixels underneath, so an arrow drawn first also appears magnified.
  • A7 Crop bakes everything drawn so far and is undoable once. After a crop the canvas is the new truth; the author is never asked to confirm a destructive step they can reverse.

22.4 Attachments age; documents do not#

A screenshot is a photograph of a version. When firmware 13.1 ships, every screenshot of the 13.0 device list is a lie that still looks true.

Text
 attachment IMG-7
 ├── data         sha256 → stored once
 ├── caption      "Device list after reset"
 ├── appliesTo    "13.0"            ← what the picture shows
 ├── referencedBy AS-8812 rev 7     ← who points at it
 └── state        fresh | stale | orphan
  • S1 appliesTo is set when the image is inserted (the document's version at that moment), and it is editable.
  • S2 A version change (a release, or the automation in §22.5) marks every attachment whose appliesTo is the old version stale, in the document and in a review queue.
  • S3 Stale is a warning on the page, not a block. Publishing a stale screenshot is allowed and recorded.
  • S4 An attachment referenced by nothing is shown as orphaned rather than deleted silently.

22.5 Automation: an agent proposes, a person approves#

The stakeholder ask is "MCP / GitHub actions generate changes automatically as we do new versions". The honest shape of that is a proposal loop, not a write-through.

Text
 firmware tag v13.1 pushed
        │
        ▼
 GitHub Action: docs-drift
        │  1. run the docs tooling in CI
        │  2. ask the MCP server for the affected assets
        ▼
 ┌───────────────────────────── MCP tools ─────────────────────────────┐
 │ docs.find_version_refs(from, to)      → assets + line hits          │
 │ docs.get_asset(id)                    → current revision + body     │
 │ docs.propose_revision(id, patch, why) → a draft revision, not a save │
 │ docs.attach_image(id, png, caption)   → attachment + reference        │
 │ docs.list_stale_attachments(version)  → screenshots that lie         │
 │ release.notes_from_commits(range)     → a draft release note         │
 └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
        │
        ▼
 Pull request (or a review item in the app) containing:
   · proposed revisions with a diff
   · the reason ("13.0 appears 7 times; 3 are firmware gates")
   · stale screenshots listed
        │
        ▼
 a person approves  →  publication  (never the agent)
  • G1 Automation never writes to a published revision and never publishes. It proposes.
  • G2 Every proposal carries its evidence: the commit range, the matching lines, the MCP call that produced it.
  • G3 The same loop runs without CI — the editor has an "Automation" surface that shows the proposals and applies them as ordinary revisions, so the feature is useful on day one.
  • G4 An agent may attach an image (a generated diagram, a re-captured screenshot) only through docs.attach_image, which applies the same size and format rules as §22.1.

Shipped: .github/workflows/docs-propose.yml. It runs on any v* tag (or by hand), derives the version pair from the tag, scans the configured folder for the old version, uploads a report and a markdown summary, applies the replacements on a branch and opens a draft pull request. It has no path that writes to the default branch, and no path that publishes. The scanner is inline in the workflow because this repository forbids new .js files — a scanner outside the tree is a scanner that rots silently.

22.6 What "a very good editor" means here, concretely#

Not a feature list — a set of properties that can be tested:

Property Test
Typing never loses the caret type 20 characters in the middle of a paragraph; selection is where the author left it
Paste is one keystroke a screenshot goes from clipboard to annotated and inserted without a dialog chain longer than one
Save is one keystroke ⌘S writes a revision; the tab never shows a dirty dot it cannot clear
Nothing is lost by opening open, close, zero revisions
Every image has words no attachment reaches a publication with an empty alt
The reader can tell truth from history a stale screenshot is labelled where it is read, not only in an admin screen
A callout shows what it claims drag over a region; the inset is that region magnified, not a stock box
Nothing irreversible is one click away crop is undoable; nothing is deleted, only superseded

22.7 What is built#

§22 is no longer only a design. The editor it describes ships as the Temco Markdown surface of extensions/temco-docs — a custom text editor on Fluent UI v9, default for *.md, with capture, annotation and the paste matrix in the surface and the file still the document. The implementation record — the protocol, the caret rules, the defects that only a real window showed, and the deliberate deviations from this section — is modules/temco-docs/extension-design.md, and the real-window evidence is the temco-markdown-editor scenario (nine steps, all passing).

Of this section's rules, the ones that now ship:

Rule Where it lives
§22.1 one pipeline for every image src/attachments.ts — one landing path for a paste, a capture and a file picked from disk
§22.2 the paste matrix the surface: an image opens the annotator, HTML tables and lists become Markdown, plain text stays text
§22.3 the annotation surface webview/docs/annotate.tsx — arrow, box, ellipse, callout, redact, blur, numbered step, crop, undo
§22.4 S1 appliesTo at insert time recorded from the release workflow's version-report.json
§22.4 S2 a version change marks pictures stale staleImages() over the record, reported by temcoDocs.staleScreenshots
§22.4 S3 stale is a warning, not a block the report records; nothing refuses a publish
§22.6 typing never loses the caret the three rules in main.tsx, asserted by check-docs and by the scenario
§22.6 the editor a person actually writes in outline, find and replace, link to a page, page properties, list continuation, indent, colour behind the words, a draggable split and three view modes — the features the text editor had and the default editor did not

Three parts of this section remain design only: the attachment state machine (fresh / stale / orphan), the publish preflight that reads the record inside the build rather than beside it, and §22.5's proposal loop, which is shipped as a workflow (.github/workflows/docs-propose.yml) but has not yet run against a real release.

23. One-paragraph brief for the generator#

Build TEMCO Platform inside the existing VS Code fork. The shell is VS Code and must not be touched; every screen we own is a webview built with React 19 and Fluent UI v9 from extensions/temco-ui, themed by bridging --vscode-* variables into a Fluent theme. Office documents are edited by ONLYOFFICE, behind a pluggable OfficeTransport: either a Document Server embedded as a single cross-origin iframe (JWT-signed config, key derived from (assetId, revision, options), short-lived signed content URL, save callback that writes an immutable revision), or a fully embedded build with static web-apps plus x2t.wasm where conversion happens in-process and no server exists at all. Markdown has two hosts — a Fluent editor by default, the same Office host when the asset remembers that choice in preferredHost — resolved by explicit override → preferredHost → setting → format priority. The feature under construction is documents (§22): a markdown editor where a screenshot goes from clipboard to annotated and inserted in one keystroke, every image is an attachment with a caption and a version it depicts, and version changes arrive as proposals from CI that a person approves. The domain is five concepts — Product, Asset, Editor Host, Publication, Knowledge — and no sixth noun may appear. Every save is a revision; nothing edits in place; nothing ever shows a blank iframe.

ui/app-flow.title: The application flow
ui/app-flow.html:
Superseded for the Docs center. The window layout, the Pages tree, the journey and the Publish flow are defined in redesign.md. Where this page disagrees with it, redesign.md wins.

The information architecture as built: the left toolbar, the four panels, the page in the middle, and the one right-hand panel. This is the confirmed design — authoring-flow.md is the capture stage inside it.

Left toolbar#

Text
 ┌─────┐
 │  ⧉  │  Explorer          VS Code's own
 │  ⌕  │  Search            VS Code's own
 │  ▦  │  Dashboard         projects · overview · needs you · recent activity
 │  ▤  │  Documentation     pages · project · pipeline · working set
 │  ⧉  │  Repositories      org → repository → code files
 │  ✦  │  AI                models · drafts waiting
 │  ◫  │  Learn             site · delivery
 │  ▥  │  SQL Studio        query & browse · schema & maintenance
 │  ⚙  │  Settings          profile · platform
 │  ?  │  Help              learn · support
 └─────┘

The shell's ORDER holds the eight module containers (temcoDashboard · temco · temcoRepos · temcoAiHub · temcoLearn · temcoSql · temcoSettings · temcoHelp); Explorer and Search are VS Code's and come first.

Dashboard — four views#

View What the panel shows The page behind it
Projects (temcoProjects.projects) a row per project: sources · built · current, with ✎ and ⓘ clicking a row opens the project page (temcoDocs.projectPage): counts, sources, outputs, build buttons
Overview (temcoWorkbench.platformView) the facts as rows — Pages · Reviewed · Stale · Issues · Sources · Outputs · Build each row opens its page (the tree, the report, Problems, the project form, Build Center)
Needs You (temcoDocs.queue) the queue's groups; a group opens its page the queue page (temcoDocs.needsPage): screenshots to place, retake these, never reviewed — each with its act
Recent activity (temcoWorkbench.activityView) the activity row the activity page (temcoWorkbench.activity): every recorded event, newest first
Text
 DASHBOARD                                        ⟳
 ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │ PROJECTS                                              ＋        │
 │   T3000 Documentation          3 sources · built 12:04 · current│
 │                                                [ ✎ ] [ ⓘ ]    │
 │   My First Docs                1 source · never built          │
 │   Legacy Import                1 source · built 09:12          │
 ├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
 │ OVERVIEW                                                       │
 │   Pages      318       Reviewed  304                           │
 │   Stale       14       Issues    0 · 3                          │
 │   Sources      3       Outputs   Site · help                    │
 │   Build      Build Center                                       │
 ├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
 │ NEEDS YOU                                               (7)    │
 │   ▸ Screenshots to place (1) · Retake these (4) · Never… (2)    │
 ├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤

 │   Recent Activity                        20 events              │
 └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

✎ = Edit the Pages (temcoProjects.openProject) → the project becomes the one being worked on and the Documentation panel shows its tree. ⓘ = Show the Project (temcoProjects.showProject) → the Documentation panel comes forward at its Project section.

Documentation — four views, the tree first#

Text
 DOCUMENTATION · T3000 Documentation          ＋  🗀  ⇩  📷  ⎘  ⟳  ⋯
 ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │ ▾ T3000Webview-EEZ-Studio            318 · folder              │
 │   ▾ t3000                            142                       │
 │     ▾ bacnet-api                       3                       │
 │         Screen JSON — Format Reference      stale · no 📷      │
 │         Point Types                         never reviewed     │
 │         Trend Logs                          ✓                  │
 │     ▾ data-points                      5                       │
 │     ▸ features                        10                       │
 │   ▾ legacy                            12                       │
 │ ▾ T3000 Docs Mirror                  128 · read from GitHub    │
 │ ▸ T3000 Legacy Archive                 — · no local copy [ ⇩ ] │
 ├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
 │ PROJECT                                                        │
 │   Sources  3                                                   │
 │   Outputs  Site · Offline help                                 │
 ├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
 │ PIPELINE                                                       │
 │   ⚑ Review Center      2 drafts waiting                  →     │
 │   ▶ Build Center       site ✓ 12:04 · help ✗             →     │
 │   ⬆ Releases           13.0 published                    →     │
 ├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
 │ WORKING SET (6)                                                │

 └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Title bar: ＋ New Page · 🗀 New Chapter · ⇩ Add a Source · 📷 Capture · ⎘ Paste · ⟳ Refresh.

The page and the right panel#

Text
 ┌ DOCUMENTATION ────┬ Data Points API.md ──────────────────┬ DRAFT ────────────────┐
 │ ▾ t3000           │ [ B  I  H2  •  ❝  </>  🔗  📷 ]      │  Draft from…          │
 │   ▾ bacnet-api    │                                      │   ◉ a source file     │
 │       Screen…     │ # Data Points API                    │   ○ another page      │
 │       Point…      │                                      │   ○ a commit range    │
 │ PROJECT           │ Points carry a scale factor.         │ ────────────────────  │
 │   Sources 3       │                                      │  Model · prompt v3    │
 │ PIPELINE          │ ![Trend log setup](media/02-…)       │  [ Draft the Page ]   │
 │   Review · Build  │ 1 Trend log list  2 Period  3 Filter │  Result (diff)        │
 │ WORKING SET (6)   │                                      │  [ Apply ][ Reject ]  │
 └───────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────┴───────────────────────┘

The rule: the right panel holds what you consult while working in the page — DRAFT for a documentation page, SCHEMA for a SQL query. Everywhere else it is closed.

What the page is, for every row#

Left panel row Page in the middle
a project row the project page — counts, sources, outputs, build buttons
Overview · a fact row the page it counts: tree · report · Problems · project form · Build Center
Needs You · a group the queue page
Needs You · a capture the attach prompt: which page takes it
Needs You · retake / never reviewed the page, with its image
Recent activity · a row the activity page
a tree page the page, in the editor, DRAFT on the right
Project · a source that source's page
Project · Outputs the project's edit form
Pipeline · Review / Build / Releases Review Center · Build Center · Releases
a Working Set row the page
a repository row the repository page
a model or a waiting draft the AI page
a SQL table row SQL, with the statement filled in

The flow#

Text
 ①  DASHBOARD · PROJECTS  ＋  → name · source (folder) · output (site)
        └─ the row appears, selected
             ├─ [ ✎ ] → DOCUMENTATION · tree
             └─ [ ⓘ ] → DOCUMENTATION · project + pipeline
 ②  DOCUMENTATION · ＋ New Page → location · kind · title → one file
        ├─ the row lands in the tree; F2 renames it
        ├─ [ Run the generator ] → it becomes a page
        └─ the page opens; Ctrl+Alt+S / Ctrl+Alt+V put a screen in its media/
 ③  DASHBOARD · Recent activity shows the build, the capture, the review
 ④  DOCUMENTATION · PIPELINE → Review Center · Build Center · Releases

Two decisions worth naming#

A row's F2 renames the file, and keeps the old id as an alias. The page id is the path (05-content-and-registry.md, rule 1), so the rename is the named act that rule allows: the file moves, the repository's own docs:registry writes the new entry, and the old id is written into that entry's aliases before anything else happens. Shift+F2 renames the title instead, which is the registry value. A project with no generator is refused — without one there is no entry to carry the alias, so the rename would orphan every inbound link.

The right-hand panel is DRAFT. It lives in the auxiliary bar and is about the page in front: Draft a Change asks what the model may read (this page's history · a source file · another page), and the drafts waiting for that page are applied or rejected there — the same commands the Review Center runs.

Needs You replaced the workbench's Needs Work view. They were the same question asked twice; the queue has real rows (captures with no page, stale pages, never reviewed) and the old view had one link.

Still open#

  • Annotation, which waits on the callout decision in authoring-flow.md (a webview's DOM, Windows UI Automation, or by hand).
  • A version-report.json writer in the product repository's release workflow: this application reads the file, and shows its pages on the project page and in Needs You, but nothing writes it yet.

ui/app-layout.html:
What the extension looks like inside Temco Platform — the shell's panels are unmodified, and only two of the five areas are ours.

Text
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Temco Platform  -  T3000Webview-EEZ-Studio                                           │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│   │ CONTENT             │ data-points.md              Preview │ TEMCO AI          (local AI) │
│   ├─────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────┤
│ ▣ │ ▾ t3000             │ 1  # Data Points API                │ You   summarise this page    │
│   │   ▾ api-reference   │ 2                                   │ AI    This page lists the API│
│   │     Data Points API │ 3  Read and write the data points   │       points; 14 months old. │
│   │     Database Mgmt   │ 4  of a controller. Each point has a│       Two points are missing.│
│   │   ▾ trends          │ 5  type, a unit and a scaling.      │                              │
│   │ ! Gaps              │ 6                                   │ [ Draft update ] [ Ask area ]│
│   │                     │ 7  Point . Type . Unit . Scaling    │ local  qwen2.5-3b  -  offline│
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ PROBLEMS   OUTPUT   TERMINAL                                                                 │
│ !  data-points.md   Order 20 is used by more than one page in "api-reference".               │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│   335 pages - 12 issues - 341 never reviewed         Markdown  -  Ln 3, Col 1  -  UTF-8      │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Panel What it is Whose
▣ Content the docs tree: areas → chapters → pages, counts on the right, Gaps at the bottom ours — the only view that does not exist in ordinary VS Code
Editor the page: plain Markdown, no front matter, Preview beside it the shell's
Temco Docs the AI: chat about the open page, Draft update, Ask the area, and which model is loaded ours
Problems structural faults only, each naming the file to fix ours
Status bar pages · issues · never reviewed mixed

Three properties of this layout are decisions, not accidents:

  1. The only new real estate is the Content view and the AI panel. Search, source control, compare, terminals, Markdown preview and the problem list are the shell's, already there, nothing to build.
  2. The AI is a panel beside the page, not a separate application. It reads the page you have open and the registry; Draft update writes a normal edit you review — so accepting is a diff, rejecting is Ctrl+Z.
  3. Both of the module's areas exist now. The Content view came first and the AI panel after it, and the mock above is the panel as built — same place, same buttons, so the layout never had to move.

Two worlds, and the seam between them#

The dashboard is not in this application. 00-architecture.md puts it on the site: a generated static page at /_admin/ — coverage · stale by owner · docs-owed · unowned pages · broken links · feedback · help-id coverage — noindex, excluded from the PDF, the help file and the offline copy, and produced by the product repository's own pipeline (the admin report task in 13-implementation-plan.md). Nothing in this extension generates it, and nothing here writes into it: the design's rule is that those are generated pages, not documentation.

What the extension does in that relationship is be the hand-off target. A dashboard row deep-links into the editor (vscode://file/…), and this is where the page gets fixed:

Text
┌── PRODUCT REPO ── the content lives here ──┐    ┌── THE EDITOR ── Temco Platform / plain VS Code ──┐
│                                            │    │                                                          │
│  docs/t3000/**            the pages         │    │  ▣ Temco Docs            (activity bar, ours)       │
│  docs/help/registry.json  the structure     │    │   ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  scripts/docs-*.mjs       the generators    │    │   │ CONTENT                                          │   │
│                                            │    │   │  ▾ t3000                                         │   │
│ ┌─ TEMCO LEARN — the site (ships) ───────┐ │    │   │    ▾ api-reference                               │   │
│ │ /t3000/13.0/…   everything published   │ │    │   │      Data Points API   (wrong order)             │   │
│ │ /feed/*.xml      changelog + releases  │ │    │   │        └ why: Order 20 already used              │   │
│ │ downloads/      PDF · help file · zip  │ │    │   │    ▾ trends                                      │   │
│ │ /t3000/13.0/    a pinned version       │ │    │   │  ! Gaps (12)                                     │   │
│ └────────────────────────────────────────┘ │    │   └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                            │    │                                                          │
│ ┌─ AUTHORING SURFACE (never ships) ──────┐ │    │   ┌─ right side ──────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│ │ :8080   docfx preview — authoring only │ │    │   │ TEMCO AI                               (the AI)    │   │
│ │                                        │ │    │   │ You  summarise this page                          │   │
│ │ /_admin/         GENERATED REPORT       │ │    │   │ AI   This page lists the API points; 14 months    │   │
│ │   coverage · stale by owner ·          │ │    │   │      old. Two points are missing.                 │   │
│ │   docs-owed · unowned · unreviewed ·   │ │    │   │ [ Draft update ] [ Ask the area ] [ Models… ]     │   │
│ │   broken links · feedback ·            │ │    │   └───────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│ │   help-id coverage · health score      │ │    │   ┌─ bottom panel ────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│ │   noindex · out of PDF/CHM/zip         │ │    │   │ PROBLEMS  OUTPUT  TERMINAL                        │   │
│ │                                        │ │    │   │  ! data-points.md   Order 20 is used twice        │   │
│ │   each row  ──►  vscode://file/…  ─────┼─┼────┼──►  the page opens in the editor, ready to fix           │
│ │   each row  ──►  the hosted editor       │ │    │   └───────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│ │                  (served by the tool)  │ │    │                                                          │
│ └────────────────────────────────────────┘ │    │   status bar:  335 pages · 12 issues · 341 never reviewed │
│                                            │    │                                                          │
│                                            │    │   Build the Site · Build the Offline Help                │
│                                            │    │     └── invoke the *product repo's own* scripts          │
└────────────────────────────────────────────┘    └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
The dashboard answers "which pages need work across the organisation?" — on the site, generated by the product repo, page-level health, never shipped
The Content view answers "which pages need work in the repository I have open?" — in the editor, one repository, the reasons as children of the page that has them
The same pages, two distances. Neither is a copy of the other, and neither recomputes what the other owns
This extension is where the work happens — a dashboard row is a hand-off, not a destination

Start a Registry appears where it applies rather than in a title bar: as the Content view's empty state, for the folder that has no docs/help/registry.json yet. It works on a folder you have open — a repository you have not cloned is refused in words, because starting one there would be a commit made through the API on your behalf. Filling the registry it creates is the repository's own generator's job (npm run docs:registry).

Where the AI sits, and why that is a user action. It belongs on the right, beside the page being worked on. VS Code has no contribution point that places a container there — contributes.viewsContainers accepts activitybar and panel only — so the view is contributed to the panel container and the workbench docks it on the right: the secondary side bar accepts any view, remembers the position, and a fresh install needs one drag. If it must open there by itself, the alternative is an editor-area webview panel opened beside the page (ViewColumn.Beside), which is a tab rather than a dock. Recorded in platform-design.md, not hidden here.

ui/application-design.title: The application: shell, screens and flow
ui/application-design.html:
The record of the agreed shape of Temco Platform as an application — the regions of the window, the screens, the way one leads to the next, and the two rules the design is built on. It is the design of record: a surface that disagrees with it is either a bug or a proposal to change this file.

Confirmed 2026-10-27. Decisions and their reasons are in What was decided; the work order is in Order of work.

To use the application rather than design it, read introduction.md: the same flow as numbered steps, with the button for every page and the command id behind it.

The two rules#

  1. A VS Code view is native. The workbench draws a tree view; an extension cannot put Fluent inside one. So the left panel is a Fluent header + chips + footer (a webview view) above a native Pages tree. The tree keeps reveal, drag, multi-select, keyboard and accessibility for free — the parts where re-implementing costs the most and shows the least.
  2. One project is one window state. Switching project re-reads and lands on the dashboard. Nothing keeps describing the project that was open before.

The publish journey#

Text
create project ─▶ add source ─▶ registry ─▶ write ─▶ validate ─▶ BUILD ─▶ RELEASE ─▶ DEPLOY ─▶ EXPORT
                                    (S6)      (S7)     (S6)      (S10)     (S11)     (S12)    (S13)
  • Build renders the registry itself: dist/site/<page>.html from marked, one stylesheet, sitemap.xml (only when the GitHub remote gives a real address), .nojekyll. A project that already has its own docs:site / docs:build script keeps using it — the generator is the fallback that makes "a folder of .md files" buildable.
  • Release freezes releases/<version>/ and records it in the catalog (already built).
  • Deploy commits the built site to the branch Pages serves and pushes it — a plain, fast-forward push, never a forced one: if the branch holds work this build does not know about, that is reported instead of erased. The commit is made in a throwaway repository whose only parent is the branch's tip, so the project's own working tree is never touched. The one-time Pages switch (Settings → Pages → Source: branch “gh-pages”, folder “/”) is attempted through the gh CLI when it is installed, and printed as two clicks when it is not. Why not Actions: the generator reads the documentation registry, which only exists inside this extension, so a CI job cannot run it. An Actions workflow would need a second copy of the renderer inside the project — a copy that goes stale the first time either side changes. CI publishing becomes possible again the day a project owns its own renderer; the branch push is what makes publishing work until then.
  • Export is local and dependency-free: the site as a .zip, any page as one self-contained HTML file, the pages and their media as a Markdown bundle. The zip writer is in the module (src/zip.ts, store + deflate over a CRC32 table) rather than a dependency, because an export a colleague cannot open is not an export. .docx needs a writer package (mammoth is import-only) and is still owed.

Temco Learn#

Temco Learn is its own module (extensions/temco-learn, the tenth), because a reader-facing website is not the same job as keeping a page in step with the code. The website itself is a separate repository — temcocontrols/temco-learn, Vite · React 19 · Fluent UI v9 · Markdown — and this module is a client of that checkout: it runs the site's own servers, builds it, shows it, writes new builds into it, and commits the result. Nothing about rendering the site lives here any more, so the site can be worked on, built and published by someone who never opens the editor.

temcoLearn.siteRepo names the clone (empty means ~/Temco/temco-learn). Everything below is a fact about that folder:

  • content/<project>/site.json — the project's title, section and summary; content/<project>/<version>/*.md — the pages a person writes, with front matter for the title;
  • public/imported/<project>/<version>/ — a project's own build HTML, copied in as it came out;
  • public/catalog.json — the one file both the website and this module read. npm run catalog folds the two sources above into it (order, titles, versions, builtAt), so the panel cannot list a page the site does not have. A second reader of a second shape is how a panel and a page start disagreeing;
  • package.json scripts — client-dev (Vite, with reload), build (catalog + search index + tsc + vite build), serve (the built pages), catalog, search, check. Neither server script names a port: the module passes --port, so there is one port for both and one setting that moves it;
  • .github/workflows/pages.yml — a push at main builds the site and hands dist to GitHub Pages. The built site is never committed: what is published is the source and the catalog it generates.

The module runs the site, it does not re-implement it. src/siteRunner.ts spawns the repository's own serve script through npm, tracks one server on one port (1025 by default), and treats "starting" as distinct from "running": it polls the address until it answers, so a frame is never pointed at a port with nothing behind it. Stop kills the process tree and waits for the port to go quiet, because npm hands the server to a child that can outlive the kill. A dist that was never built is built before the built pages are first served, rather than served as an empty folder.

Preview is a panel framing the running site (src/preview.ts, temcoLearn.site.preview), with a bar over the frame that is a caption, not a toolbar: a tinted strip (--vscode-sideBar-background, 34px, one hairline under it) holding the state as a coloured dot and one word, then the address, then the acts — and every one of those is a link, not a box, so nothing in the strip competes with the website below it. No address bar, because the address is not a question: one port, set once, and a person who wants the site is not choosing a URL — but the address is clickable, because what a person does with a URL is click it, and it goes where the act beside it goes. The three acts read Reload · Open in Browser · Stop: the second one is named for where it goes rather than for the noun Browser, which said what the thing is instead of what the button does. Reload and Open in Browser are inert with no address; Stop never is. Closing the panel does not stop the server, the way closing a browser tab does not stop a website; Stop does. Add This Build to the Site copies a build into public/imported/<project>/<version>/, writes the site.json the catalog needs (the title comes from the build's own <title>), runs npm run catalog, and shows the new version — only the version is asked, and it is asked once, in the version box, never in a notification. Publish commits the clone and pushes it at main; it refuses a folder that is not a clone instead of initialising one, because an empty history pushed at a real site is worse than a refusal.

The panel is three views in the container, the way Home is three — VS Code draws the header, the separator and the collapse state, so the grouping is the one a person already knows from the Explorer, and each section carries its own title-bar actions. A row is a name and a glyph, and what it holds is TreeItem.description — the grey words the Explorer writes beside a folder (3 versions), never a badge of our own. Sentences live on the Overview page and in tooltips, never in a row.

view rows the grey words
Overview one row, Temco Learn, which opens the page —
Site Preview the Site (a state dot and one word; its heading opens the Site page; Stop/Start, Open and Open in Browser :1025 under it), then Library (one row per project, at its newest version) the state: Running, Starting…, Stopped, Failed, Not set up; projects served
Artifacts one row per project built on this machine, opening onto the files its build wrote; Publish closes the view (initialSize: 4) nothing — the name only, and a hover carries the count and the paths; Publish puts its count at the row’s right end

Three views, one subject each. Artifacts is content: the files the builds on this machine wrote, plus the single act that is about all of them at once (Publish). Nothing here is a task list and nothing here is a state — a view holds things, and the things are files.

Adding a build is not in the panel at all, because it is a site operation: it copies a build into the site repository and asks for its version, exactly like cloning, building and publishing write into that repository. So it lives on the Site page, as a section of its own — Builds not on the site, one row per build with the reason it waits (not on the site, newer than 13.0) and one Add… button — and every command that means "add a build" (temcoLearn.addBuilds, from the Overview callout, its workflow card, the Publishing page's step, the + on the Site view) opens that page with the section first and marked. That is the whole answer to "what is that row for": it is the step that turns a folder on disk into a version on the website, it needs the version typed, and it belongs beside the other steps on the site.

Build a project is not a row either: building happens in Temco Docs, so it appears only when nothing has been built at all — Nothing built on this machine yet / Build a Project… — where it is the honest next step. The ellipsis is VS Code's signal that a click leaves this window, and the tooltip says where it goes.

A label is navigation or an instruction, and the two are not the same sentence: a button on a page that goes to the other module reads Open Temco Docs (the way VS Code says Open Settings), while the last row of an empty view reads Build a Project…, because a view with one line in it has to answer what do I do, not what opens.

Site answers two questions, in that order. Preview the Site is a group whose heading is the page and whose children are the only acts a panel is good for: Stop while it is running and Start while it is not (one row, the word swapping with the state), then the two places the site can be read — Open, a tab in this window, and Open in Browser, which shows the port alone (:1025) — and both start the server first if it is down. The two are named for the difference a person feels, not for the API behind them: Open stays here, Open in Browser leaves for the browser they already have. Everything else a clone needs — clone, pull, install, build, change the folder or the port, the log — is the Site page's, because a second copy in the panel is how a panel and a page come to disagree about what is running. A clone that is not there swaps those rows for Clone temco-learn… and Use an Existing Clone…, and the heading says Not set up and still opens the page that explains it.

The heading's glyph is the state, not the site: a filled circle in charts.green while it serves, sync~spin while it comes up, error in charts.red when it failed, circle-outline when it is stopped, cloud-download in charts.blue when there is no clone — the way VS Code's own Ports view draws a running process, so a glance down the panel answers is it up? before a word is read.

A row's facts sit at the row's right-hand end, and in a tree that is a decoration badge and nothing else: description is drawn inline, immediately after the name, so it can never be a column — but a badge is a ::after on the label element, which is a flex row, so it is the last flex item and lands at the edge (views.css even gives it a 4px right margin). RowDecorations answers one badge per row of the module's own scheme: Running/Stopped/Failed/Not set up in the state's colour, :1025 on the browser row, 2 projects on the library. So the three rows read as a table without a single space character of padding, and the words are in the tooltips as well, for anyone who has turned badges off. The provider answers synchronously: a decoration that arrives as a promise leaves the first paint of its row blank, because DecorationsService only has the data when it is already there.

Library is one row per project, at its newest version (T3000 · 13.0), opening that page on the site at #/<project>/<version>/ and starting the server first if it is stopped. Not one row per version: a product with twenty versions turned the panel into a scroll bar, the newest is the one a person wants nine times in ten, and the site's own list holds the rest. The name is Library because the rows are documentation sets, not pages — a page lives inside a version, and a category is the catalog's section field, a different axis. The row writes the project's name, without the "docs" a build's own page title usually ends with (Test1 docs reads Test1 · 1.0), and it carries no description: the version is already in the label, and a grey 2 pages beside four rows was the noisiest thing in the view. A site with nothing on it does not report emptiness: its one row is Add a Build to the Site…, which runs the same picker the view's title bar does. There is deliberately no group of dist builds: the build as written is a file on disk, which is the Artifacts page's business, not something to read here.

The Site page is where the clone is managed (src/sitePage.ts, temcoLearn.site.page), and it is what Preview the website opens when there is no clone — a folder dialog was never an explanation. It reads the folder every time it is drawn (src/siteFacts.ts: branch, commit, ahead/behind, changed paths, node_modules, dist) and offers the act for each answer: clone into ~/temco/temco-learn, use an existing clone, change the folder or the port, pull (--ff-only, never a merge), install, build, start, stop, open a terminal, and clear or open the log (src/siteLog.ts, the same bounded ring the publish page keeps). The runner grew the two git steps the page needs (git, pull, clone), so a clone and a pull print into the same log a build and a server do.

The page is a control panel, not an article, and it names itself Documentation Site — Site said nothing the view title did not, and Temco Learn above it was a breadcrumb of one, which is a label pretending to be navigation. The title block says what the site is (its own repository, the toolchain, one port) and the state (Running · localhost:1025 · built, Stopped, Failed), then one primary act chosen by that state — Clone → Install dependencies → Build the site → Start the site → Open, with Try again when a start fails. Open goes to a tab in this window; the title carries the globe chip, because it is the page of the site and the browser is what it shows.

The site is read in two places, and the page names both the way the panel does: Open in the This machine row stays here, Open in Browser leaves for the browser the reader already has. A button labelled Open that opened a browser was the ambiguity worth removing; the tooltip on each says which one it is.

A failure is said once, at the top, in the tinted callout — with the reason and the two acts that answer it (Try again, Open the full log). The title block then says only Failed; saying the reason twice made the reader look for the difference between two identical messages.

The clone's own facts are not in the sentence. A meta line under the title block carries them, in mono, and pairs them with the two figures that say how far the copy has drifted — 0 commits behind origin, 5 paths changed — so they scan as numbers with left edges in a column rather than hiding at the end of a paragraph. The repository, the commit and the changed paths are links (a command, never an href): the first two open GitHub at that commit, the last opens the Publishing page, which is where those paths are listed. A clone with nothing changed links nothing — a link to an empty list is a dead end:

0 commits behind origin        5 paths changed

Below that, the page is two parts, and both section titles wear the brand's vertical rule (the shape the Overview page uses):

part what it answers drawn as
This machine what is here, and is it running the server as one line — state in mono, Repository │ Terminal, then Start/Stop, Open and Open in Browser — then four small cards in one row: Folder · Port · Installed · Built (two across under 760px). A card is a label, a value and the act that changes it, with no border: its condition is a 6px dot in charts.green when the step is done, charts.yellow when it is not, and a hollow one when there is no condition to report
Activity what it said a tabbed area, Output and Publish, plain text on a tint off the card surface: no border, no header bar, no line numbers. The tabs are radios and labels, so they switch with no script and still answer the keyboard

Log was the wrong word, and so was Console — a log is a file, and this is what the module did: a clone, a pull, a build, a server, and the last publish. It used to be two places as well: pressing Build opened the preview panel to report on itself, so a build either pushed the site out of the way or the message was lost. Every message now goes to the page that owns the button (say / complain in src/extension.ts), which is why the area has two tabs: Output is this window's command lines, Publish is the publish page's log, which a person used to have to leave the page to read.

Every line is cleaned before it is drawn (cleanLine): ANSI colour codes stripped (an escape sequence arrives as ΓÇö in a console that is not a terminal), control characters dropped, the module's own [site] / [git] prefixes and the $ prompt removed, and the glyphs a build or a dev server uses to decorate its output (➜, ✓, box drawing) taken out — the words they decorate are kept. The raw lines stay in the output channel, where a terminal is the right place for them.

One port, one way of serving. serve listens on 1025 (temcoLearn.sitePort, above 1024 so it binds without root on macOS and Linux) and shows dist/ as it was last built. There is no second mode: client-dev — Vite with hot reload — exists for editing the site's own React and Markdown, which is the repository's business and not something this page decides, so a terminal still runs it (npm run client-dev -- --port 1025). A page that serves what was built has one way to serve it, and a switch that changes nothing for the reader is a question nobody asked. A change to the port takes effect the next time the server starts, and the log says so.

Publishing is one page and one press (src/publishPage.ts, temcoLearn.publishing). The row reads Publish the Site — the count is already at its right-hand end as a badge, so the label says what is published and the number stays a number. The row opens the page rather than acting on the click, and the page has four sections, each with the 2 px brand bar:

  • The repository — one card, not a band of four cells. A head line of links (the remote opens the repo on GitHub, the commit opens that commit, the branch sits plain between them), then 12 paths in this commit and the first five of them, each a link to the file on GitHub. The rest fold into a native <details> — Show 7 more paths — so a publish that touches forty files reads as six lines and expands in place, with no script and no round-trip. The foot says whether anything is unpushed and offers Open the clone · Terminal.
  • What publishing does — the four step cards, each ending in the act that performs it.
  • Where it goes — one card for the one subject: ADDRESS as the page's biggest link (it opens the live site), then Served from (main, built by GitHub Actions, handed to Pages), Last publish and Waiting as label/value pairs.
  • The last attempt — the lines git printed, unchanged.

The button that does it (temcoLearn.publishNow) writes its result where the decision was made, so there is no preview strip to read it in and no second page to be redirected to.

Artifacts has a page (src/downloadPage.ts, temcoLearn.downloads), opened by the Artifacts view's empty row and by its title bar. Three sections, each with the 2 px brand bar the other pages carry: What a build writes (five cards — the website, the help file, the pdf, the archive, the Word document), Where it lands (one card, because there is one working area: the folder written out as the card's own link, and two lines spelling out <project>/dist and the HelpDocs folder), and The files on this machine (a grid of file cards per project, packed from the left at the width the content asks for — minmax(215px, 240px) with justify-content: start, because letting them stretch put one file in a card 900px wide — each with the glyph for its kind, the name, offline help · 1.1 MB, and the two acts a file on disk has: Show in the folder for every card, and Save a copy where a copy can be taken). Look used to sit there and drew the viewer into the inventory; looking at a .pdf or the built site is the panel's job and the OS's, so the card finds the file instead and gets out of the way.

The page lists only what a build produces as a whole. A loose .html in dist is a page someone was iterating on, not an output: listing it beside T3000.pdf made the page read like a folder dump, so it is filtered out — and a project whose only result is such a fragment is not a project here at all, which is why the count in the title block counts the cards rather than the files on disk. The panel's Artifacts view draws the same line: it lists what can be taken away, never a fragment. Publish closes that view as Publish the Site — the count sits at the row's right-hand end as a badge, and the tooltip carries the last publish. Publishing is about every build at once, which is why it is the one act that sits with them.

Nothing is invented: a project with no .chm has no .chm row, and the panel says Nothing built on this machine yet only when nothing exists at all. Publishing state is read from git (src/state.ts) in the clone, so two machines never disagree about what is out.

Answers appear in the preview's own strip, under its bar, and never in a notification: adding a build, building, publishing, and every failure say what happened there, with at most one thing to do next. Only the inputs stay native — the version box, and the build picker when a row did not name its build, and the folder dialog for a clone that has not been chosen yet.

Settings → General is a bundled Fluent page (webview/settings/, React 19 + Fluent UI v9), not markup generated in the extension host: the tokens are Fluent's, the brand is Azure's blue, and every control is a real Fluent control. It is drawn in the house page language rather than a settings template — the brand wash with an eyebrow, a title and a note; one tinted callout; a section heading with the 2px Azure rule before it; an entry row per setting with its control at the right-hand end; a facts band; and links at the foot of the last block. main.tsx imports temco-ui's media/page.css, so the wash, the rule, the row and the buttons are the same rules Temco Learn's Overview page is drawn by and the two pages cannot drift.

The host's half is narrow: src/settingsPages.ts builds the bundle when a source tree has none (a compile wipes out/), hands the webview settings.js and settings.css under a content-security policy that allows nothing else, and answers three messages — ready with one state, setting with a key to write, command to run. A refresh is a new state and never a new document, so a write does not throw away the reader's scroll. npm run build-webview builds it; build-webviews and vscode:prepublish run that too.

Design system#

  • Fluent v9 (@fluentui/react-components, @fluentui/react-icons) with the brand ramp seeded from Azure blue #0078D4 through createLightTheme / createDarkTheme, following VS Code's light, dark and high-contrast through data-vscode-theme-kind. The package named Azure theme (@fluentui/azure-themes) is v8/Fabric and does not apply.
  • Tokens: spacing 4 / 8 / 12 / 16 / 24 · radius 4 / 6 / 10 · type 20 / 16 / 14 / 13 / 11 · row 22 (compact 20) · status colours taken from the VS Code chart colours, so a chip, a dot and the status bar cannot disagree.
  • Row anatomy, one component reused everywhere: [icon] title · meta · status dot · hover actions.
  • Page anatomy: the title block (one h1, one line of why, the ways in), then sections whose titles carry a 2px brand bar to their left, then at most one tinted callout, which is the thing a person would do next. Figures live beside the thing they are about — a stage of a pipeline, a row in a list — never in a strip of tiles whose only label is the number itself.
  • A list folds, it does not truncate: the first five rows are shown and the rest are behind a native <details><summary>…</summary>, so the count in the heading stays true.

Order of work#

  1. Generator ✅ — src/siteRender.ts (pure: slugs, page shell, index, sitemap, one stylesheet), src/site.ts (host: read, render, write, copy media), scripts/check-site.mts (10 cases); Build the Site falls back to it.

  2. Deploy ✅ — src/pages.ts (the remote decides the sitemap's address) and src/git.ts shared with the diff command. The push of a site lives in temco-learn (src/publish.ts: ensureRepo refuses a folder that is not a clone, then a plain, never-forced git push origin HEAD:main; scripts/check-publish.mts, 5 cases against real throwaway repositories); temcoDocs.publishSite stays behind as a redirect. Still owed: the status-bar state and the confirmation screen S12.

  3. Export ✅ — src/zip.ts (a real archive writer: store, deflate, CRC32), src/export.ts (site zip, single-file page, Markdown bundle; temcoDocs.export + three commands), scripts/check-export.mts (5 cases that read the archive back). Still owed: .docx. Then the panel.

  4. Panel and shell — (in progress) the activity bar is five entries ✅; the Project strip above the native Pages tree ✅ (src/panelView.ts, check-panel.mts); the status bar ✅ (src/statusLine.ts, check-status.mts); S3 (the project dashboard) ✅ inside the Project Detail page: pages · drafts · stale · issues, a Needs you group, and Last out of the building; S13 ✅ as the Exports page (temcoDocs.export opens it; the three shapes are still their own commands, plus .docx from src/docxWrite.ts — Word's format is a zip of XML, so it needs no dependency); S12 ✅ folded into the Releases page as Where It Publishes; S1 ✅ the Projects page opens itself when the window is on no project and has no tab; S6 ✅ as The Registry page — every entry with the reason it might not appear in the site, and one action per reason; S10 ✅ the generator reports its steps (Resolve → Render → Assets → Sitemap) to the notification and the output channel as they happen; S11 ✅ publishing a release confirms first, naming version, destination and file count.

    Phase 4 is done, and so is every gap the screen audit found. What remains for the shell is the tabbed Ship surface (Build · Release · Deploy · Export as one page) — deliberately not built: after the cross-links and the Exports page, the four surfaces point at each other, so it is polish rather than a gap. The status line deliberately carries the window's facts (project · pages · issues) and not the version or the last build: those need the catalog, and a catalog read on every file save is too high a price for a status bar. The strip in the side bar shows them instead, from a render that already had a reason to read the catalog.

Overview is an application page (src/overview.ts, view type temcoLearn.overview), drawn with temco-ui the way every other page of ours is, and it is never published. It opens with the sentence that says what the module is for — Temco Learn publishes the documentation website — continued by the counts it reads from the snapshot (3 projects are published today, 7 versions and 42 pages between them) so no project name is ever written into the prose. Then, in this order: one callout for what needs doing (or that nothing does, or that nothing has been built yet); Publishing workflow, four cards — Build · Add · Publish · Download — one line each, ending in the link that performs it (Open Temco Docs, Choose a build · 1 waiting, Publish · 3 changes, Show in the folder); and Where it stands, three lines, one per page that acts on the facts they name. The section headings carry the 2 px brand bar the other pages use.

And it stops there — with one line back. The page used to go on with three parts — Published projects, Build outputs and Publication — that restated what the pages which act on those facts already say: the Site page holds the clone, the versions it serves and where it is published; the Artifacts page holds what a build wrote; the Publishing page holds the address, the branch and what a push would carry. A summary page that copies the page it summarises drifts from it, so the lists went. What came back is Where it stands, and it is deliberately one line per page rather than a section per subject:

line the fact on it it opens
Documentation Site 2 projects · 3 versions · 4 pages the Site page
Artifacts 3 files · 5.3 MB the Artifacts page
Publishing https://temcocontrols.github.io/docs/ · 3 changes waiting the Publishing page

A count is the one thing worth repeating: it is computed from the same snapshot on every draw, so it cannot drift, and it answers "is there anything in there?" without a list that has to be kept in step. Each line ends in the standard Open ›, so the detail is one click away and lives where it is edited.

Add a build is a section of the Site page, not a panel view: it belongs to the page that clones, builds, runs and publishes the site, because it writes into the same repository those do. Builds not on the site lists every build on disk whose project is absent from the catalog or whose dist/site is newer than the version the catalog lists, each with the reason (not on the site, newer than 13.0) and one Add… button. Adding asks for the version, copies into public/imported/, runs npm run catalog, and publishes nothing. Every command that means "add a build" opens that page with the section first and marked. Nothing about it is automatic: a test build stays out of the public site until somebody adds it. A link on this page is text with a glyph (temcoLearn.* command), never an href into the website — that boundary was crossed once already. The module therefore depends on temcocontrols.temco-ui, exactly as temco-docs does.

A build is not one thing. temco-docs writes the site (dist/docs or dist/site), an offline help file (.chm, inside the repository or in a HelpDocs folder beside it), often a .pdf, and the exports it keeps in dist/ — a zip of the site, a Word document, single pages. src/artifacts.ts reads those three places per project and reports what is there: nothing is invented, so a project with no .chm simply has no .chm row, and a file in a shared HelpDocs folder belongs to the project it is named after. Each artifact is either something to look at (site, chm, pdf, a single page) or something to take away (zip, docx, and the files that are both), which is the divide the panel draws.

The panel (src/tree.ts) is three views in the order the questions are asked — Overview (one row: the page above), Site (Preview the Site with a state dot and the port, and Library with one row per project at its newest version), and Artifacts (a project, and the files its build wrote — names only, with the size and the path on hover; a row saves a copy and offers Show in the Folder inline; Publish the Site closes the view, its count at the row's right end). What a row holds is its description: the grey words beside a name, as the Explorer writes them — and where a row deliberately says nothing, the hover carries it.

ui/authoring-flow.title: The authoring flow
ui/authoring-flow.html:
Superseded for the side bar layout. The Docs side bar (Pages, Needs You, Sources, Publish) is defined in redesign.md. This page remains the record for the screenshot capture stage only.

The design for screenshots in the authoring loop, and for the side bar that had to change because of them. This is the record the next round argues with, so that a redesign starts from a decision rather than from the previous screenshot.

The reference#

The bar is Dr.Explain, and its loop is not "a documentation editor with an image button":

capture a running window → its controls become numbered callouts → write one line of text per number → export the same topics to CHM, PDF and the web.

Two properties make that work: the screenshot is taken of a window, so the callouts can be placed by the machine instead of by hand; and every artifact is built from one set of topics. Before this change we had no capture stage at all, so the side bar had filled the space with destinations that were not places in the documentation — Projects, Areas, Pipeline, Working Set.

The flow#

Text
 T3000 is running — the thing being documented
     │  Ctrl+Alt+S  capture a screen          Ctrl+Alt+V  paste from the clipboard
     ▼
 CAPTURE     the screen becomes a file
     ▼
 TOPIC       the page being written; the file lands in that page's own media/
     │       NN-area-slug.png · ≥ 1600 px · ≤ 2 MB · type sniffed, never trusted from the name
     ▼
 TEXT        the body, with the reference at the cursor
     ▼
 GATE        registry · links · media audit · width · the version a page describes
     ▼
 BUILD       the product repo's own scripts → the site, and the offline help
     ▼
 NEW VERSION version-report.json → "retake these" rows → Ctrl+Alt+V again

Stages 1 and 3–5 exist and are untouched by this change. Capture was the missing stage, and it is now built as far as it can be without the callout decision below.

The rule that places every feature#

The question a feature answers Where it lives
"Where in the docs am I?" the Pages tree
"What am I writing right now?" the page and the editor's toolbar
"What is waiting for me?" Needs You
"What am I shipping?" one Build & Release page, reached from the tree's title bar
none of the above it does not belong in the product

What changed#

The tree gained a home of its own; the Documentation panel kept the groups it had.

Surface What it is
Documentation panel (temco) Projects · Pages · Areas · Pipeline · Working Set — as before
Documentation Tree (new activity-bar container, temcoDocsTree) Pages — the documentation tree, the same provider as the panel's Pages view
Needs You — the queue below it: screenshots with no page yet, pages the code moved away from, pages never reviewed

One provider behind both tree views, so there is still one answer to "what is the documentation". The menus on the panel's Pages view apply to the tree view as well.

Needs You lists only facts something else already computes, and every row runs a command that already existed:

  • screenshots with no page yet, from the capture inbox;
  • pages the product repo marks stale (read, never recomputed);
  • pages never reviewed, as one row with a count and the report behind it.

Screenshots are a stage. temcoDocs.captureImage (Ctrl+Alt+S) opens the Windows snip overlay and takes what it puts on the clipboard; temcoDocs.pasteImage (Ctrl+Alt+V) takes an image that is already there. Both then:

  1. find the page in front — the active editor's page, else the row the tree has selected;
  2. write into that page's media/ as NN-slug.ext, the number continuing the folder's own sequence;
  3. insert ![title](media/NN-slug.ext) at the cursor, or at the end of the page when it was not open;
  4. warn — not refuse — below 1600 px wide, and refuse outright above 2 MB.

With no page in front the screen is not guessed at: it goes to <root>/.temco/captures/ and waits in Needs You until Attach the Screenshot to a Page… puts it where a person says. The inbox is outside every media/, so the site only ever holds what a page shows.

temcoDocs.chooseImage is the third path, for a file that is already on disk; it is the one that also works outside Windows.

Why reading the clipboard needed no change to the core#

The extension API reads the clipboard's text and not its image — docs/temco-platform/ui/editor-design.md §3 said so, and it is still true. But this application is Windows, and System.Windows.Forms.Clipboard reads the image with no native module and nothing installed: what Win+Shift+S, PrintScreen, Snipping Tool and every other capture tool leave behind. So the limit is a platform fact rather than a wall, and it costs one PowerShell child process per capture.

What is not built, and the decision it waits for#

Annotation. Crop, arrow, box, text and blur/redact, saved over the capture, with the untouched original kept aside so a retake is diffable. It is a contained piece (a canvas over the captured image), but it contradicts 15-online-editor.md, What is not built — "a screenshot is captured properly or not at all" — so it is a rule change that needs to be taken deliberately, not slipped in with a button.

Automatic callouts, the Dr.Explain core. It depends entirely on what is captured:

What the screen is of What can be placed automatically
our own webview T3000 callouts from the real DOM elements — this is Dr.Explain's magic, nearly free
the classic Win32 T3000 control bounds from Windows UI Automation — automatic, but coarse
a device screen, or a customer's machine nothing; manual crop, arrow, box, blur is the whole feature

The answer decides whether the annotator is a callout tool or a drawing tool, which is why it comes before the annotator.

The version report. docs/help/version-report.json — version, changed areas, affected pages, images older than the version they describe — written by the release workflow, read by Needs You and by Build & Release, consumed by the MCP server. Designed, not built; it needs no UI of its own.

Order#

  1. The two views — done.
  2. Capture, paste and the inbox — done.
  3. The callout decision, then annotation in the page.
  4. Build & Release as one page: the build, review and release commands that exist today, in one place.
  5. version-report.json, then the Action and the MCP wrapper.
